Apple today announced that App Store prices for apps and In-App Purchases will be adjusted in five countries starting December 3, following changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates. Here are the details.

In a new post published on its developer portal, Apple today announced a series of changes to App Store pricing, as well as updates to tax rules affecting developers and customers in several countries, including the US.

According to the company, developers’ proceeds from eligible app and In-App Purchase sales have been adjusted in four countries, reflecting the following tax updates:

Specific to Botswana and Rwanda, Apple said that “Exhibit B of the Paid Applications Agreement will be updated to indicate that Apple collects and remits applicable taxes.”

Apple added that a new “Software as a Service (SaaS)” attribute is now available for several App Store tax categories, including App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting. Developers can review and update their tax category selections in App Store Connect.

Additionally, starting December 3, developers who rely on Apple’s automatic pricing adjustments will see changes to app and In-App Purchase prices in:

Apple usually makes these adjustments to account for changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates, and notes that prices won’t change in countries selected as the base storefront, for auto-renewable subscriptions, or in storefronts where developers manually manage their prices.

The announcement does not go into detail about how much prices will change in each country, or whether they will increase or decrease.

Finally, starting January 1, 2027, apps and In-App Purchases in the SaaS, App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting categories will become subject to sales and use taxes in California.

Apple noted that “prices on the United States storefront are displayed to customers exclusive of taxes, so the tax change will not affect them,” but added that while developers’ proceeds will remain unchanged, “the total amount customers are charged, inclusive of tax, may increase.”

I have many gripes with modern smartphones, but one of the things that really grinds my gears is the trend of Godzilla-sized camera bumps on the backs of phones, Apple's doing it, Samsung' seems to be planning on it, and a lot of Chinese brands look like they've been hit by a rogue hockey puck. I've been testing the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, which also has a large, iPhone-looking camera bump, but this time things are different.

Xiaomi has taken on the task of making the most out of that normally-wasted space on the camera bump by turning it into a screen. This is not the first phone to feature a rear-mounted screen, or even the first Xiaomi flagship to do so, but in a world of phones that all seem to feel and look the same, it's quite exciting to see a phone company offer something that helps its phones stand out.

But the question is not whether the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's Back Display is interesting, it's whether it's able to justify its own existence.

Looking at the 18 Pro Max, my mind immediately jumped to the cover displays on compact foldables. The way the display wraps around the two main cameras is reminiscent of the Galaxy Z Flip 8 and the Motorola Razr. It's a little smaller than those screens, measuring 2.9-inches compared to those 4+-inch screens, but all three share a common purpose.

This is a way to use your phone without actually using your phone, using the smaller screen to look at basic information like the time or notifications on a smaller and more power-efficient display. At the same time, and as Xiaomi is keen to emphasize, it's a way to customize the look and feel of your phone in a way that cases and other accessories just can't manage.

My initial thoughts upon looking at the back of the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max and playing around with the screen weren't totally positive. I couldn't stop comparing it to the cover screens on foldable phones, and the fact that those screens are front-and-center when you take out your device. Xiaomi's screen is on the back, which is not part of my phone I tend to pay very much attention to.

But the more I used it, and the more I figured out that it wasn't just a glorified clock and notification alert, the more I realized that my initial reaction was the wrong way of looking at things.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The idea that this is potentially a very valuable feature clicked when I opened up the camera on the Back Display. This allows you to take selfies using the main cameras, in a similar fashion to foldable phones, using the rear-mounted screen as a viewfinder. This means you're taking selfies with the 200MP main camera, rather than the lower resolution hole-punch camera on the front.

I'm not going to lie, though. This isn't a fully-fledged phone screen capable of running all the apps and services that you've got installed. It is significantly more limited than that, and the difference is like describing the difference between a smart home hub and a tablet.

The home hub may be useful for its own specific use case, but it doesn't have the same versatility or usefulness as a tablet running Android or iPadOS.

The Back Display is great for glancing at notifications and the time, especially if you tend to leave your phone lying face down. It even supports Live Activities on a handful of apps, including letting you control music playback on Spotify. Plus, it's possible to customize your screen with different backgrounds and clockfaces, depending on what your own personal tastes and style might be.

So far so good, though I can't say that I've ever felt using my main screen for those tasks has ever been a particular burden — especially since I'm just not used to looking at the back of my phone.

Then again, if you already have a smartwatch, that's not going to mean much, since you already have the bulk of this information available on your wrist.

Xiaomi does seem to be hinging on Generative AI to turn this screen from a gimmick into something you'll want to use throughout the day, thanks to a built-in system that lets you vibe code your own apps.

Anyone that remembers the flop that was Windows Phone will know that success of a mobile platform hinges on app support. Your apps give the system value, and without developers actively contributing to an app store, there's little reason for people to actually invest in one of your devices.

So how do you get app developers on board to add utility to a niche display on the back of a handful of phones? You don't. You hand that job to the users, and let generative AI do all the hard work. So Xiaomi added a prompt-based system for creating Back Display apps from scratch, as well as an App Store of sorts that lets you see a curated selection of what other people have created.

Options I can see include workout schedules, mini games, educational tools, timers, and all kinds of different options, though I have no idea how effective or accurate they actually are compared to full-coded apps. Still, it's nice to see that there's a way to improve the usefulness of the Back Display — even if it would be nice to have proper Android apps on offer.

I found that basic prompts did work, but the more detail you could offer the better the outcome. Xiaomi can "polish" your prompt to better your chances of generating a usable app.

However, this does not guarantee that the app would successfully generate — or that it would work. It took me multiple attempts to create a Doom clone, and even when it did, I kept getting killed off by a monster hiding out of my line of sight.

So it's not quite as painless as having a developer-made app, and playing games on a small screen isn't ideal. But in the absence of additional features, this system is fairly good at filling that niche.

I've spent my entire life looking at the front of my phone, and never really concerning myself with what's on the back. Even in the pre-smartphone era the screen was everything, whereas the back was just... not important. If rear screens start to take off, that could change the way people interact with their phones in a big way. And that's obviously going to take a lot of getting used to.

That's probably the biggest hurdle these rear screens will face. There's certainly no shortage of utility, especially with the generative AI apps. It's just reprogramming user habits to glance at the back of the phone rather than looking at their main display. It's going to be an uphill battle to convince people that these screens are worth it, especially when they have to compete with wearables.

If it weren't for the AI apps I'd say these screens don't have much of a chance. I'm not convinced that they will take off, aside from a few niche gimmicks, but at least they have some sort of unique selling point to work with.

#3396. The UK and some other countries don’t get more Siri AI usage with iCloud+

Apple this week revealed the additional Siri AI usage you’ll get if you have an iCloud+ subscription. This ranges from doubled limits for a 200GB plan to 20 times for a 12TB plan.

However, the company’s support document reveals that some countries will not get access to these increased usage allowances …

Apple hasn’t yet specified the standard limits applicable to Siri AI usage, instead saying that these will vary depending on anything from the feature used to the overall level of demand at the time. However, it did list the proportional increases you get with paid iCloud plans.

However, tucked away in the small print in the company’s support document are some exclusions. One of them is no surprise: EU countries.

Siri AI isn’t available at all in the EU due to Apple’s perception of potential antitrust issues. Essentially, Apple believes that if it launches Siri AI there, it will be required to give competing AI services the same level of access to its devices. But three other countries are specifically excluded:

Apple gives no explanation, simply saying:

Increased access to Siri AI with iCloud+ is subject to Siri AI availability and is not available in Brazil, the EU, UK, or South Korea.

However, I have a strong suspicion about the reason.

What all three countries have in common is that they’ve taken a strong antitrust stance with Apple on a number of occasions over a range of issues.

It may be that Apple has genuine concerns about how regulators might respond if they effectively throw in free access to increased Siri AI usage. The company may fear that this would be viewed as anti-competitive by implicitly disadvantaging other AI services.

A less charitable take would be that Apple is firing a warning shot across the bows of these countries, seeking to communicate that there are consequences for what it views as attacks on its ecosystem. If customers are angered by missing out, Apple might be hoping that these feelings would be directed at regulators rather than the iPhone maker.

What’s your take? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3394. There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen."

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

#3393. Banks, FAA, Microsoft, Apple – no systemic attack on the US, says White House

A set of major tech outages in close succession is leading some to speculate that they are connected, and that the US is under systemic attack by a hostile state.

All the evidence suggests otherwise, with individual explanations for each of them – and the White House is now saying as much in a bid to put fears to rest …

Whether there was or wasn't a cyber attack, I wouldn't believe a single word from the White House.

On Thursday, a widespread Microsoft 365 outage ran into the following day when two unrelated issues coincided. Friday saw a nationwide ground stop of US air traffic due to a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centers. On Monday, a bug in a Chase bank system saw disruption not only to the bank itself, but also other banks where Chase was a party to a transaction. Finally, yesterday saw many Apple services offline, with retail stores also affected.

The Apple outage doesn’t appear to have been significant enough to have reached the administration’s radar, but CBS News reports secretary of state Marco Rubio saying the others are unrelated.

“The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we’ve seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another,” Rubio said […]

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind. Each of them are distinct, and they’re different in their causation.”

The statement was backed by Senator Mark Warner.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, also said on Tuesday that there’s no indication these incidents are the result of an attack.

Warner went on to say that the ability of AI systems to find vulnerabilities at “unprecedented speed” does, however, mean companies and government agencies alike need to be ready to patch vulnerabilities immediately.

#3391. MacPaw’s Moonlock comes to iPhone, helping users detect potential scams

After launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today. Here are the details.

When MacPaw launched Moonlock on the Mac, the company described its new app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”

In practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats. Users can also manually scan their Mac for malware, including suspicious files hidden in system folders and email attachments.

Beyond that, Moonlock includes a VPN to encrypt internet traffic, a network inspector that shows where apps are sending data and lets users block connections to specific countries, and an AI-powered scam detector that analyzes messages pasted into the app for signs of phishing. It also helps users review and adjust macOS security settings.

Today, MacPaw is launching Moonlock for iPhone, a move the company says “helps people recognize potential scams, understand their iPhone’s security and take practical steps to improve it.”

Unlike the Mac version, Moonlock for iPhone doesn’t scan for malware, as iOS prevents third-party apps from accessing other apps and their files. Instead, it focuses on identifying potential scams, checking for exposed personal information, and helping users improve their iPhone’s security.

On the iPhone, Moonlock lets users quickly check suspicious texts, screenshots, and QR codes for phishing, in addition to checking whether their email addresses have appeared in known data breaches.

As MacPaw explains it, Moonlock’s Scam Detect “helps people check suspicious messages they encounter throughout the day. Whether it’s a text message, a screenshot shared by a friend, or a QR code, users can paste, scan or share content directly with Moonlock and receive an assessment explaining why something may be suspicious.”

Here’s Oleg Stukalenko, Head of Product Management at Moonlock by MacPaw, on today’s launch:

“When we launched Moonlock, our goal was to make cybersecurity something anyone could understand and use. But so much of what people do today, from banking to everyday conversations, happens on their phones. Bringing Moonlock to iPhone felt like the natural next step. We want to help people spot a scam before they tap, see where their security stands, and know exactly what to do next.”

MacPaw adds that Moonlock for iPhone also includes the following features:

MacPaw’s Moonlock for iPhone is free to download, with subscriptions available for $9.99 per month or $49.99 per year.

#3388. Six new Aqara smart lights with Apple Home support and ‘spatial intelligence’

Aqara has announced the global launch of six new smart lighting products with full Apple Home support and what the company describes as “spatial intelligence.”

The new lineup includes a vertical floor lamp with 18 individually addressable lighting zones, and a new LED strip offering seamless color gradients, dynamic flowing effects, and music synchronization …

All of the new products are Matter compatible, allowing them to fully integrate with Apple Home, in addition to supporting the full range of competing ecosystems: Amazon Alexa, Google Home, Samsung SmartThings, Home Assistant, and Homey.

With a compatible sensor like the FP400, all of the new products support spatial intelligence.

This enables automation to respond not only to whether someone is present, but also to exactly where people are within a space and how they move through it. For example, the ambient lights can turn on and off based on your movement from the couch to the dining room table.

Its intelligent AI sensing algorithm drastically improves reliability by reducing false triggers caused by environmental factors like pets, airflow, and robotic vacuums. A built-in ambient light sensor also helps trigger smart home scenes based on both human activity and lighting conditions.

You might initially struggle to spot the new products in the company’s new releases section on its Amazon store. That’s because instead of each having its own section, you need to click or tap on the product in the top image.

Pricing ranges from $24 for new light bulbs through to $320 for the 100-foot-long permanent outdoor rope lights. You can find all the new products here.

#3386. The Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess adds new color grading sets, expands to iPhone

VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone.

VWFNDR + MBL launched on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out. A unique UI that adapts to the shot, minimal processing for a natural look, and support for DNG files at a level that only Google’s Pixel Camera app can truly compete with.

The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial update.

On Android, this comes in the form of new color grading profiles built into the app. “NATURAL,” “NIHON,” or “B+W.” The app still saves an unprocessed DNG alongside the JPG and the grading adapts across the frame rather than having a fixed result, keeping highlights and shadows in place.

Colour grades: MBL still records unprocessed Bayer RAW DNG, and the JPG it renders alongside now uses one of three grades: NATURAL, NIHON, or B+W. Grading happens on VWFNDR’s own spatial engine. Instead of applying a fixed LUT, it adapts across the frame, much like a raw editor, so highlights and shadows keep their detail. The DNG stays untouched.

The rest of VWFNDR + MBL 2.0 takes place off of Android.

In a rare case of the tables turning, MBL was released first on Android, and only on Android for the first several months. But VWFNDR is now bringing the app to iPhone with support for variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro and Content Credentials, Apple’s version of the C2PA standard that’s meant to prove a photo is real and not AI-generated.

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is one of the most comfortable pillows I’ve tested for Tom's Guide, and more than lives up to its luxury $135 price tag. A shredded memory foam and latex fill hugs your head while supporting your neck no matter the position you sleep in. Lacks firm support for tall and heavy bodies

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Saatva is the luxury sleep brand behind the number one rated option in our best mattress of the year guide, the Saatva Classic (see our Saatva Classic mattress review), which is why I'm always eager to test the Saatva's sleep accessories that deliver the brand's signature luxury for less. Along with its mattress toppers and bed sheets, Saatva also offers a line-up of premium pillows, one of which is the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow.

Filled with shredded gel-infused memory foam, the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow promises universal support and comfort — so I tested it for a week to see if it's worthy of a place in our best pillow guide.

Despite the name, the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow isn't made completely out of memory foam; it also contains natural latex. And after testing it for a week, I'm happy to say that if I’m going to sleep on a memory foam pillow, I want to sleep on this one.

Type: Memory foam and natural latexBest for: Combination sleepers and hot sleepersSizes: queen and king, standard and high loftTrial: 45 nightsWarranty: 1 yearPrice: $135 at Saatva

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is sold in a standard and high loft with a breathable cotton cover that’s removable and washable. Inside the cover is a mixture of memory foam and natural latex pieces that create a comfortable and huggable pillow. The shredded foam design worked well with the cotton cover to prevent any overheating at night.

I tested the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow in a standard loft and, though I sunk slightly into it, the pillow seemed to settle to the perfect height needed to sleep comfortably on my back and stomach.

While I could sleep on my side on the standard loft, I would suggest the high loft for side sleepers who need more support. This pillow gave me no reason to doubt its durability as it always returned to its shape when I got up in the morning.

A starting price of $135 does push the Cloud Memory Foam Pillow into the premium price tier, but it's not completely surprising for a luxury sleep brand like Saatva. However, you can sometimes catch a bundle deal that can save you up to $60 when you buy two.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is breathable and comfortable for all sleep types. Starting at $135, it’s a luxury buy, although for Black Friday you can save when you buy a pair of pillows. Buyers also receive a 45-night trial and one-year warranty when they order this pillow.

A standard queen size Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is $135, which puts it into a premium category. Saatva rarely, if ever, includes pillows in the monthly Saatva mattress sales, but it sometimes has cut-price deals on a pair of pillows during sales events such as the Black Friday mattress sales.

In fact, the current Saatva Black Friday mattress sales have a deal where you can save up to $60 when you buy two Cloud Memory Foam Pillows at Saatva.

If this pillow was filled solely with memory foam, I’d say it was overpriced. The natural latex added to the fill and a cotton cover make the price feel more reasonable, though I think a removable fill to make the height adjustable at home would make this pillow feel like better value.

Saatva offers a 45-night trial and a one-year warranty with the purchase of this pillow. Brands like Bearaby only offer 30-day trials, so an extra 15 days is nice, until you consider the generous trial offered with the Coop Adjustable Latex Pillow — 100 nights and 5 years warranty for some of its latex pillows.

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow can be ordered in two sizes – queen and king – and two loft heights — standard and high. The standard loft is 4"-5" tall, while the high loft is 6"-7" in height.

This pillow has a breathable organic cotton knit cover (though it doesn’t have organic certifications) that’s removable and washable.

Despite the name of the pillow, the fill is comprised of both shredded gel-infused CertiPUR-US memory foam and natural latex foam. According to Saatva, the Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is hypoallergenic.

I slept on the Helix Cooling Memory Foam Pillow for a week and performed a series of objective and subjective tests, following our pillow testing methodology.

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow arrived in a clear plastic bag within a cardboard box. It wasn’t vacuum sealed, meaning when I pulled it out of the plastic bag, it was ready to be slept on.

There weren’t any noticeable off-gassing smells when I pulled it from the packaging, but to be fair, I was really congested during the testing period because of hay fever.

However, when I slept on the pillow, there was an almond smell to it, which is a fairly common off-gassing scent for memory foam products.

The previous Saatva pillow I tested was too tall and didn’t have much give — which is why I breathed a sigh of relief the first time I laid my head on the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow.

I tested a queen standard loft and discovered it to be the perfect size for someone like me who likes to sleep on her stomach, back, and side.

The shredded fill of this pillow spreads when weight is placed on it, but not enough that my head sunk down to the bed.

As I moved my head on the pillow, the pillow felt malleable and soft, hugging my head in a comforting way. I particularly like how this pillow feels when I’m lying on my back and stomach, as my head sinks enough to align my spine, lulling me to sleep quickly.

I can sleep on my side with the standard loft size. However, I think the high loft would be better if I was strictly a side sleeper.

When the pillow eventually breaks down, I can see myself sleeping on my side less and less with this pillow and reverting to my back or stomach. Those with broad shoulders should choose the high loft size from the get-go.

I placed a 15lb weight in the center of the pillow, and it sunk over an inch. That makes sense considering the foams inside are shredded. When I lifted the dumbbell, the pillow sprung back into shape immediately, which is a good sign of the its durability.

I didn’t wake up hot or sweaty when sleeping on the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow, and that’s all thanks to Saatva’s temperature regulation. Memory foam is a far more heat-retaining material than natural latex, so to mitigate any overheating issues, Saatva utilized organic cotton for the cover — which is breathable — and shredded the memory foam and latex interior fill so air could weave its way through and keep my temperature neutral at night.

During the beginning of testing, I was sleeping without the air-conditioner and just a fan, so it was about 75 degrees in my house when I fell asleep at night and around 70 degrees when I woke up in the morning. The fact that heat did not build up during that time was very promising, and most likely what you can expect throughout the year.

A good rule of thumb: replace your pillows every two years and keep an eye on how quickly your pillow bounces back over time.

This can be done by folding your pillow in half. A slow bounce back means the fill has worn down. Until the pillow breaks down, maintenance will ensure it lasts longer.

After a week of testing, I haven’t noticed any sagging or break down of the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow. The shredded nature of the memory foam and latex fill means you may not be laying your head on the same bits of foam each night, which will probably result in a longer lifespan.

The cotton cover also appears durable, and if well maintained (i.e. washed) it should hold up for at least two years. If it does break down, you could easily replace the cover, but I don’t see that happening.

Thankfully, Saatva offers a one-year limited warranty on this pillow so if you notice anything out of the ordinary, take advantage of the warranty.

It wasn’t until I was an adult that I realized how important it is to take care of your pillow. They easily absorb sweat, night creams, and all manner of stuff from your head and face. Maintenance ensures they last longer.

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is made of two parts — the cover and the fill. The cover can be removed and machine washed on cold on a delicate cycle, and either hung to dry or tumbled dry on low.

You can’t throw the memory foam and latex fill into the wash, but you can spot clean it if you need to.

Comfort is the most important thing to me when it comes to a pillow and the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow delivered.

The cloud-like and huggable surface is conducive to a good night’s sleep, especially since it’s supportive enough to keep your head and spine aligned no matter what position you sleep in. If you prefer to sleep on your side, I would order the high loft option, as it’ll offer more support for a longer period of time.

The cotton cover and the shredded natural latex and memory foam fill results in a breathable design, so you won’t sleep hot or sweat at night.

During the testing period, the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow bounced back quickly, leading us to believe that it’ll last the full two years of a pillow's lifetime. Especially if you wash the cover consistently.

All in all, this supportive and huggable pillow will cradle your head and lead to a comfortable night’s sleep.

✅ You overheat at night: This pillow is breathable, thanks to a cotton cover and an interior fill of shredded latex and memory foam.

✅ You're a combi sleeper: This pillow has the right amount of give and support for those who like to sleep on their stomach, back, and side. I suggest the high loft option for side sleepers.

✅ You like to try your pillow for a decent amount of time: Saatva lets buyers test a pillow for 45 days. If you don’t like it, Saatva will accept a return and give you a full refund.

❌ You prefer organic materials: This pillow does have some memory foam and while it’s CertiPUR-US certified, that doesn’t mean its free of toxins or VOCs, only that it’s low enough to be considered “safe.” Neither the natural latex, nor the organic cotton used in the fill and the cover are certified as organic despite claims by Saatva.

❌ You like to customize the size of your pillow: While you can order this pillow in high or low loft, unfortunately, Saatva didn’t design it so you could remove or add fill and thus adjust the height in your own home.

❌ You like a supportive, firm feel: Your head is going to sink into this soft and cloud-like pillow. For a more supportive and firm feel, try Saatva’s Down Alternative Pillow.

The Helix Talalay Latex pillow is a good alternative for those who don’t like their head sinking too far into their pillow as it’s made from a single piece of foam. Expect a bouncier feel. Made with Talalay latex and perforated with holes, this pillow will help you stay cool all night long. It comes in two loft options and you can get this pillow for as little as $111, which is more affordable than the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow.

As the name of this pillow indicates, the Coop Sleep Good Adjustable Latex Pillow is adjustable. It's made with a blend of natural Talalay latex and microfibers, and comes with an extra bag of fill so you can add more if necessary and create the loft and feel you prefer. Our reviewer reports that the pillow is breathable and prevents heat from trapping. A 100-night trial and a 5-year warranty is worth having, too.

If you want buttery soft comfort for a budget price, then I reccomend the viral Squishmallows SquishPillow, which is just $29.99 in a standard size. Currently our No 1 budget pick thanks to our glowing SquishPillow review (which praised its plush comfort and reliable support), the SquishPillow comes in a medium, firm or soft.

#3384. The Best Tech Deals From Costco's Early Black Friday Sale

Sam's Club, Walmart, Amazon, and other retailers have been churning out early Black Friday deals since last week, so if you haven't been paying attention, you've already missed out on some good deals. But all hope is not lost: Costco recently started its own early sale, so you're still in time to find something you want at a low price. Below, I've rounded up my favorite tech deals from their sale—but keep in mind you'll need a membership to take advantage of these deals.

A powerful monitor with high-end specs can make gaming more immersive and greatly reduce input lag, which is helpful for any serious gamer looking for an edge over their opponents. The Samsung Odyssey G9 is a 49-inch gaming monitor with some impressive specs, including a 240Hz refresh rate and a 1 ms response time. It's available for $699.99 (originally $899.99), $200 off and the lowest price it has reached this year.

If you're looking for a more premium (and far more massive) gaming monitor, the 57-inch Samsung Odyssey Neo G9, one of the best ultra-wide gaming monitors on the market, is currently on sale for $1,449.99 ($2,499.99 at launch). This monitor came out in 2023, earning an "excellent" review from PCMag for its impressive 7,680 x 2,160 4K resolution, its great color range and accuracy, a 240Hz refresh rate, 1,000 nits of brightness, and its overall design. To make full use of its powerful 240Hz refresh rate, you'll need to use DisplayPort 2.1, or you'll be limited to 120Hz. You'll also need a powerful graphics card. But if you have the right setup, this thing really delivers.

The 15.3-inch Lenovo Legion is a powerful gaming laptop with premium specs, and with the current $600 discount, it's down to $1999.99 (originally $2,599.99). It has a powerful AMD Ryzen AI 9 processor, 32 GB of RAM, a GeForce RTX 5070 graphics card, and 1TB of SSD. PCMag gave the more affordable 5i version an excellent review for its price and performance, so if you have the cash for it, this one is even better.

A soundbar is a great way to improve a home entertainment system without spending too much money. This 5.1 TCL Q6CH setup is currently $199.99 (originally $299.99), including a soundbar and subwoofer. This soundbar came out in 2024 and supports Dolby Atmos and DTS:X for that 3D sound, as well as AI Sonic, a tool that tunes your sound settings based on the setup of your room.

The latest AirPods Pro are a big step up from their previous generation. The third iteration of Apple's iconic earbuds deliver a number of quality-of-life and software improvements that make them worth the typical premium over the AirPods Pro 2—and right now, the AirPods Pro 3 are even cheaper than the previous generation: They're $179 at Costco (originally $249) in an early Black Friday deal.

The 15-inch MacBook Air is down to $1,249 (originally $1,499), the lowest price since Apple hiked prices this past summer. The M5 MacBook Air is the best laptop for most people looking for a new machine in 2026. In comparison to the already excellent M4 Air, the M5 base model has double the storage, and the powerful M5 chip makes the performance even smoother, according to Mashable's review. The aluminum design is as good as you'd expect from Apple's most popular portable laptop, and it includes a Liquid Retina display, Touch ID, a 12MP Center Stage Camera, and the Magic Keyboard.

The 15.6-inch Acer Aspire Go is a great value at its current $499.99 price (originally $699.99). The display is a touchscreen; it sports an AMD Ryzen 5 processor and it has 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. These aren't specs you normally find at this price, making it a great laptop for anyone looking to stretch their money as far as possible while getting a workhorse of a laptop.

I'm a fan of TCL TVs, and currently own the "non-pro" version of this TV. The 65-inch QM6K Pro is $599.99 (originally $999.99) and has the same internal hardware and Mini-LED panel as the regular QM6K, but it adds a CrystGlow anti-reflective coating that makes it more viewable in well-lit rooms and helps maintain a high picture contrast. The 144 Hz native refresh rate makes gaming smooth, and support for Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+, HDR10, and HLG means you're well positioned to get the best sound quality when streaming movies or shows.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

#3383. Leaker claims Apple developing four models of 20th anniversary iPhone

Leaker Ice Universe says Apple is currently developing four models of the 20th anniversary iPhone which we’ve been referring to as the iPhone 20. We’re expecting next year’s flagship models to be a radical new design with an all-glass appearance.

Why four models rather than two is unclear, but it seems possible Apple is testing two versions of both the Pro and the Pro Max to determine just how ambitious it can be with the final product …

Didn’t the iPhone 6 or the iPhone 11 already have a curved front glass?

Ice Universe says that two of the four models have quad-curved glass backs and two have flat glass. They indicate that Apple has already had to ramp back its ambitions with the curvature.

Apple is currently developing four models in total: two with flat glass backs and two with quad-curved glass backs. Apple has been prototyping this quad-curved design for three years, making several revisions along the way—particularly regarding the glass curvature, which is still being refined. The earliest version had a very pronounced curve; it was later reduced somewhat.

It’s standard practice for Apple to develop multiple competing prototypes of new devices, evaluating them for everything from usability and durability to ease of manufacturing.

We’re expecting Apple to use a combination of ultra-thin bezels and curved glass to create the illusion of no bezels at all – a more sophisticated version of the effect seen on the Apple Watch. Today’s report says the bezels are around 1mm thick.

The curved edges on the quad-curved version are approximately 1mm wide. However, because the glass curves around all sides, when viewed straight on from the front, the bezel becomes nearly invisible, creating a near‑borderless appearance. The actual visual effect could be quite stunning.

We yesterday saw an AI-generated render of what the design could look like. It’s expected to be the biggest redesign of the standard iPhone since the iPhone X.

#3379. How Microcredentials Can Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program pairs AI governance standards with microcredentials

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Kaitlyn Ridel is a marketing specialist for the IEEE Microcredentialing Program

#3376. Man Found Guilty of Igniting Blaze That Became the Devastating Palisades Fire

A jury found a former Los Angeles resident guilty of starting what became the deadly Palisades Fire of January 2025, the city’s most destructive wildfire in its history.

Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, was convicted of one count of destruction of property by means of fire and one count of arson affecting property used in interstate commerce. Federal prosecutors accused Rinderknecht of intentionally starting the original blaze, known as the Lachman fire. While the initial fire was quickly suppressed, unbeknownst to firefighters and other authorities at the time, embers of it continued to burn underground. On Jan. 7, heavy winds reignited the fire, causing it to surface and spread. The ensuing Palisades fire was one of the most destructive wildfires in Los Angeles history, killing 12 people and decimating 23,448 acres of land and nearly 7,000 structures across the Pacific Palisades region.

“Twelve people lost their lives and thousands lost their homes because of Jonathan Rinderknecht’s malicious conduct,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche in a statement. “Thanks to the persistence and hard work of our prosecutors in the Central District of California, he will be held accountable.”

“Jonathan Rinderknecht deliberately ignited a fire that killed 12 people and devastated an entire community,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli. “We were determined to hold him accountable, and today’s guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended.”

After a federal jury in June deadlocked in favor of acquittal in Rinderknecht’s first trial in June, federal prosecutors narrowed their case to charge him with the two arson-related felonies rather than the three charges in the mistrial.

Steve Haney, the man’s lawyer for both trials, told the Los Angeles Times that they planned to appeal Friday’s verdict. “We are disappointed in the verdict, but respect the jury process,” Haney told the publication. “After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration.” Trending Stories Patrick Stewart Cause of Death Revealed Selena Gomez Shares Her Reaction to Martin Short Ruining Her Wedding Cake ‘Yes, Dear’ Star Anthony Clark's Cause of Death Revealed Marlon Jackson Reveals Stage 4 Prostate Cancer Diagnosis Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

The prosecution argued that Rinderknecht, who was working on New Year’s Eve as an Uber driver on Dec. 31, 2024, was angry and frustrated because he was unable to find companionship on New Year’s. According to an affidavit from an investigator for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, two of his passengers described him as “agitated and angry” that night. He allegedly drove to a Pacific Palisades trailhead, where he repeatedly listened to and watched a music video for the rap song, “Un Zder, Un Thé,” about despair, and tried calling an old friend, but was unable to connect with them.Prosecutors said that Rinderknecht started the Lachman Fire just after midnight, and that around 12:12 a.m. on Jan. 1, 2025, environmental sensing platforms indicated the Lachman fire had begun. They said that Rinderknecht called 911 several times, but didn’t get through because his iPhone was out of range. By the time he finally connected with the police, the fire had already been reported by others in the neighborhood.

During his call with police, per the affidavit, Rinderknecht also allegedly typed a question into ChatGPT: “Are you at fault if a fire is lift [sic] because of your cigarette?” ChatGPT allegedly responded “Yes.”

#3374. 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?

VicOne’s AI-assisted research reveals what faster zero-day discovery means for robot safety

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety.

VicOne used AI to find 28 zero-day vulnerabilities in Physical AI tools —these weaknesses can impact robot training, testing, and real-world control.

This article is brought to you by VicOne.

VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.

Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.

These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.

Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.

When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.

VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.

Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.VicOne

The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.

These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.

In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.

Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne

AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.

An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.

When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.

As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.

That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne

Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.

#3372. iPhone Duo is getting three new features in iOS 27.3

iOS 27.3 launches next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model.

Apple is granting iPhone Duo users one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

Face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient new option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple:

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

If your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most users, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

On a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

Reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

You can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great new option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces new iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use

What should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that users have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a new setting so users can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

By default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

It’s not exactly a “new feature,” but iPhone Duo users will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

Here’s a comparison of the old and new keyboards via Beta Profiles on X:

iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z

Read more: iOS 27.3 changes the iPhone Duo keyboard, here’s how

#3371. Patrick Stewart Cause of Death Revealed

Patrick Stewart‘s cause of death has been revealed.

The beloved English actor died at age 86 on Oct. 28 in his Los Angeles home. His death was confirmed by a statement on his social media, which added that the cause was “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and lewy body dementia.”

His death certificate, obtained by People, lists cardiopulmonary arrest as his cause of death, and neurocognitive disorder with Lewy body as an underlying condition. TMZ was first to report the news.

The Emmy-winning performer, known for both his good natured persona and indelible roles in popular franchises like Star Trek and X-Men, was adored by his collaborators and the public alike. Stewart’s career spanned decades with work across more than five dozen films and over 50 television appearances, from X-Men and Star Trek to Dune and American Dad. Trending Stories Patrick Stewart Cause of Death Revealed Selena Gomez Shares Her Reaction to Martin Short Ruining Her Wedding Cake ‘Yes, Dear’ Star Anthony Clark's Cause of Death Revealed Marlon Jackson Reveals Stage 4 Prostate Cancer Diagnosis

His stage roles also ran the gamut from Shakespeare’s Scottish play to Waiting for Godot to his memorable one-man version of A Christmas Carol. In 1966, he joined the Royal Shakespeare Company and he remained with the storied company until 1982. During his tenure at the Royal Shakespeare Company, Stewart featured in numerous productions, including Hamlet, King Lear, and The Taming of the Shrew. He would continue appearing onstage throughout his career, notably joining longtime friend and actor Ian McKellen for Waiting for Godot in 2009 and again in 2014.

In a wave of tributes from Hollywood following his death, William Shatner remembered Stewart, who succeeded him as captain of a Star Trek franchise. “Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor,” wrote Shatner. “From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did.”

#3369. Six Things You Should Do Now to Optimize Your Setup for GTA 6

You’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI. You’ve preloaded the game on your console, you’ve taken the next month off work, and you’ve locked your phone in a Faraday cage and set it adrift at sea. You’re prepared to lock in, and you haven’t forgotten a thing…right? Well, just to make sure, here are the most important tips to optimize your setup before you fire up the most anticipated game of the decade.

GTA 6 is absurdly large. According to Rockstar, you’ll need up to 212GB of storage space. For high-end consoles like the PS5 Pro, that’s more than 10% of the available storage space, and close to half the space on the more budget-conscious Xbox Series S. There’s a good chance you’ll have to delete something to make room.

Alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it). External SSDs are probably the cheapest route, though you’ll want to make sure to use a high-speed USB cable to connect it. It’s even worth shopping around for alternate models of SSD. For example, at the time of writing, the popular 2TB WD_BLACK external drive was close to $200, but the exact same drive in pink was $132.

You can also directly upgrade the storage of your console with expansion drives. The Xbox Series X|S supports proprietary expansion cards, while the PS5 and PS5 Pro can accept most M.2 internal SSDs. These will generally be faster, since they plug directly into the console via higher-speed connections than a drive hooked up via USB.

Let’s face it: Half the fun of any sandbox game is the weird, unique stuff that happens to only you. So you’re probably going to be hitting that “record recent gameplay” button more often than usual. While you’re cleaning up your storage space (or adding more), make sure to account for all the video clips you might want to save.

File size of video clips depends on a lot of factors, but 4K recordings can generally take up to 0.5GB per minute of footage. You can cut that down by saving footage in 1080p instead, but either way you’ll want to leave a little extra space.

Game footage is also a pretty good place to look if you need to make room on your console and don’t want to delete any games. Be honest with yourself: You don’t need all those clips from Horizon Forbidden West you saved four years ago. Dive into the settings on your console and find the biggest media files you forgot you even had on there.

According to Rockstar, GTA 6 will be targeting 30fps across consoles at launch, which is pretty low as modern AAA games go. Part of the reason for that is all the processing power going to rendering a complex environment, but it also means you won’t need a fancy high frame rate TV or monitor any time soon to get the most out of it. Still, it couldn’t hurt to check a few settings on your display.

First, make sure you’re using a higher refresh rate than 30Hz. While the game is targeting 30fps, it is technically capable of more, so if your console can keep up, you don’t want to accidentally bottleneck your frames. This setting will vary by device, so check the manual that came with your screen.

Also, make sure you have HDR enabled on your hardware. There’s a good chance this is already turned on for your TV, but sometimes other devices can switch display modes if they only support SDR. The game will help you calibrate your HDR settings for GTA 6 specifically when you launch it, but only if it detects HDR compatibility in the first place.

If you’re planning to buy a console specifically for GTA 6, this might be one of those rare instances where a PS5 Pro really is worth the upgrade. According to Rockstar, certain features like ray-traced shadows will only be available on the Pro version of Sony’s console.

More importantly, the PS5 Pro version supports PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (or PSSR), which upscales lower-resolution images to get better detail and higher frame rates out of the same hardware. Given that GTA 6 is already starting at a meager target of 30fps on most consoles, anything that can give your frame rate a boost is probably going to feel like a welcome improvement over the baseline.

I’ll tell you a secret as someone who’s spent a lot of time testing different game controllers: Most of the time, you really don’t need an expensive “elite” controller. Most of the time. I don’t buy into the idea that a taller control stick is going to make you an esports athlete. It can be nice to have, but it’s not a game changer. What does matter is customizing your controls, especially for long gaming sessions.

The DualSense Edge wireless controller is a favorite of mine, mainly because of the rear paddles and adjustable triggers. The former lets you map any button to a rear lever that you can access with your fingers underneath the controller, which can often ease some of the wrist strain of awkward button combos. And the adjustable triggers let you activate the buttons with less motion, again reducing repetitive stress.

The Xbox Elite Series 2 controller has similar features for the Xbox, as well as custom caps for the D-pad. Both consoles’ versions of pro controllers are more expensive than the standard ones, but if you’re planning to game for many hours, it can be worth it to get a controller that’s more comfortable for you.

If you have an Xbox One, you don’t necessarily have to upgrade your console to play GTA 6, but you might want to take a look at your network. GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on day one, and you’ll be able to stream the game to an Xbox One console (as long as you purchase Cloud playtime as well or get some with your Game Pass subscription). This is the only way to play on a console older than the current generation, so if you don’t want to shell out for new hardware, this might be your best bet.

Xbox recommends a minimum of a 20Mbps connection to run cloud gaming, but more is obviously better. If you can connect your console to a wired Ethernet connection, that would be better and provide more stability. If you can’t connect a cable, then at least make sure you’re well within range of your wifi router, and try to limit any other bandwidth-hogging applications on the network while you’re playing.
