#3351. Gustavo Dudamel Enlists Dave Grohl, LL Cool J, Cynthia Erivo for Brad Pitt-Produced Documentary

I n December, Gustavo Dudamel will make his much-anticipated return to conduct the Los Angeles Philharmonic for a string of dates. It’s the first time he will head back to his former home of nearly 20 years since beginning his tenure as the New York Philharmonic’s Music and Artistic Director. Given the multiple standing ovations and chants of “Gustavo” that resonated through the Hollywood Bowl during his final LA Phil bow in late August, his arrival will be a much welcome one.

Alongside his trip back to the West Coast, Rolling Stone can exclusively announce a documentary about Dudamel and the LA Phil will premiere on Dec. 7 coinciding with his concerts at Walt Disney Hall on Dec. 4, 5, and 6. The documentary, titled Symphony of a Thousand, is described as “Set during challenging times in L.A., the film encapsulates Dudamel’s philosophy on how music can create connection and community in an increasingly fractured world.”

The Jennifer Tiexiera-directed film, produced by Brad Pitt’s Plan B Entertainment, features footage from Dudamel and the LA Phil’s pair of performances at 2025’s Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival, where they made history as the first major orchestra to perform a full set at the massive event. It features Dave Grohl,  LL Cool J, Cynthia Erivo, Natasha Bedingfield, Becky G, CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso, and Zedd. Kevin Macdonald serves as the executive producer, with producers Jeremy Kleiner, Dede Gardner, and Chloe Mamelok.

Landmark pop culture moments like this have peppered the course of Dudamel’s trailblazing career. And he wasn’t about to go (east) quietly. His final nights helming the LA Phil culminated in a weekend at the Bowl that featured the Foo Fighters and other pop luminaries, concerts that doubled as a benefit for his home country of Venezuela. A conversation at the Grammy Museum followed.

“I met Gustavo at a party about 12 years ago, and I fell in love with him. As a heterosexual man, it confused me,” Coldplay’s Chris Martin affectionately jokes when joining Dudamel and LA Phil onstage during the benefit concert for Venezuela finale. “And I realized it wasn’t so much sexual as musical in the way I just wanted to cuddle him forever. And we’ve been musically cuddling ever since.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Trailing Dudamel during his final full-time week in L.A., that sentiment carries through to every interaction. At the closed final rehearsal on a Sunday morning in August, camera crews swirl around as two women busily work to notate the score, and a handful of onlookers from the team at the Bowl gather to take in the moment in the blazing heat. There’s a hushed reverence knowing an era is coming to an end, but also smiles abound, particularly from Dudamel who warmly hugs old friends as they join him onstage.

As he conducts, he throws the full weight of his body in a stance both graceful and animated — like a kid at his first dance. His baton alights in the air and comes down, and the orchestra responds, while he swoops and sways to the music. “5/4 pum pum,” Dudamel instructs as they run through one composition. Later, Meme del Real from Café Tacvba takes the stage to rehearse the poignant “Eras.” Lasso follows with an a cappella of “En Otra Vida.”

It’s the morning after their phenomenal performance with Foo Fighters, which marked the band’s first-ever set at the Hollywood Bowl. That pairing is not an unusual one for Dudamel, though. He’s made a name for himself breaking down perceived traditional genre boundaries in his 17 years at the Bowl, where he’s collaborated with an array of artists, including LL Cool J, Christina Aguilera, and Beck, who later at the finale concert performs “Ride Lonesome.” Beck’s dad, celebrated arranger-composer David Campbell, also attends the final rehearsal. Related Content Foo Fighters, Noah Kahan, the Who Lead New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival Lineup See Foo Fighters Return to ‘Baker Street’ on ‘Kimmel’ Foo Fighters Go Back to the Start on 'Kimmel' With 'This Is a Call' Foo Fighters Play ‘Window,’ Dave Grohl Talks Taylor Hawkins on ‘Kimmel’

“If I reflect about how I feel, yes, I feel exhausted,” Dudamel tells Rolling Stone with a smile when we meet at the Grammy Museum a couple of days later. “Every day a rehearsal, every day a concert. Next day a different program, another concert.” It’s been a nonstop whirlwind, but it’s also been a time “full of beauty,” he says.

“I have the chance to dive inside of all of that amount of talent — because it’s not only the soloists that play with me; it’s all that orchestra, that 100 musicians that are there, that I have shared 17 years of my life with them, and of course it doesn’t finish,” he continues. “This goes to eternity because when you develop something that is so deep and so powerful as developing an identity through music, it’s the biggest privilege … Every single note, every single second that I have the chance to share, or people share with me, that is a privilege to have the chance to work with all of these people and to create all of this environment.”

If there are a couple of overarching words to describe Dudamel, they would be magnetic charm. When we arrive at the Grammy Museum a few hours before his event, several people rush him to ask for selfies, to which he happily obliges before he’s quickly ushered into the building. People from the music world and beyond appear drawn to him, not only for the music he helms and the open environment he’s created around it, but also for his altruism.

At intermission during Dudamel’s Hollywood Bowl finale, Coldplay’s Martin heads backstage to rehearse with YOLA, the youth orchestra inspired by Dudamel’s own experience coming up in El Sistema, the publicly-funded National Network of Youth and Children Orchestras of Venezuela. (It was there while discovering music technique that “I saw the immense and infinite possibilities of all kinds of music,” Dudamel says.) Martin asks each child their name before leading them through a warm-up and taking to the piano. He vamps his lyrics to “Viva La Vida” before the choir comes in with the buoyant Oh-oh-oh bridge. “Absolutely fantastic,” Martin tells the students. He reminds them: “Remember when we’re out there onstage, this is our band … We’re doing this together.” Later onstage, they deliver their spine-tingly performance, which prompts a crowd-wide sing-along.

YOLA, which provides free instruments and education to create social change through music, is a vital part of Dudamel’s legacy and his north star. “I grew up not in an environment of conservatory, rigid. No,” he says. “It was music as a tool of social transformation — that is El Sistema. And of course, for me, opening spaces for young people to have access to music as a tool for them to have beauty, to have creativity, to have empathy, creating together — that is for me the most important thing. And [as] artistic institutions, we have to do that … for people to see the transforming power of music.

“When you have this chance to transform your life, creating harmony, creating beauty together — when you go out as a citizen, you behave differently because you see the real dimension of connection that goes beyond any material thing, any ideological point of view, and then you are connected through the empathy of human being and doing things beautiful for others.”

As for his hopes to bring a similar program to New York and beyond, he believes it’s imperative. “We don’t have the chance in this world to contemplate, to really see each other, to create something that requires discipline, but at the same time joy together. When you are doing music, in an orchestra, in a choir, and you feel that first moment that you create harmony and that you are part of something beautiful and powerful, that enhances your spirit. I think that is the way for our kids to be inspired, especially in the chaotic but beautiful, in the only world that we have. So we have to create more spaces like this.”

As a longtime champion of crossover collaborations, Dudamel attracts artists across genres and disciplines, but a recent team-up came by way of an unusual source, via actor Bradley Cooper, who is a mutual friend of Dudamel’s and Stella Hopkins. Hopkins began sharing scores with Dudamel, which were composed by her husband, actor Anthony Hopkins. It led to them working on an album.

“The thing about musicians is that they, unlike actors, they don’t have that ego,” Anthony Hopkins tells Rolling Stone of working with Dudamel. The pair met up at the Grammy Museum to talk about their collaboration on Hopkins’ debut classical album, Life Is a Dream. Dudamel conducted London’s Philharmonia Orchestra for the project, which comprises work Hopkins has composed over the course of more than six decades.

During his Venezuelan benefit show, Dudamel and LA Phil performed Hopkins’ “Stella Aria,” a moving ode to the actor’s wife, which featured a beautiful solo from Venezuelan cellist Gregorio Nieto at the concert.

“It is a great honor and a privilege because he actually endorsed my music,” says Hopkins. “I mean, I’m always filled with self-doubts as we all are … I have no theoretical, technical, musical training as such — everything is instinctive from childhood. So, naturally in me is the — ‘do I, is this good enough?,’ But when I sat there and Gustavo got up onto the podium to conduct the massive orchestra there, and I was astounded as the sound came out. He’s playing my music. Did I write that?’”

Dudamel has a knack for making artists feel comfortable in new situations as his next act in New York illustrates — it has begun, unsurprisingly, with rave reviews. In September, his premiere debut with the New York Philharmonic at Radio City Music Hall drew the kind of rock star lineup one would expect from Dudamel. Hosted by Liev Schreiber, it featured Lizzo, St. Vincent, and Joaquina. “The Philharmonic plays for Dudamel with visible investment and enthusiasm,” a New York Times review of his first week’s New York concerts reads. “Its members haven’t looked this happy onstage in years. Either he inspires them, or his starry arrival has lifted their morale. Or both. Whatever is going on, it works.” Trending Stories Watch Buffalo Springfield Come Together for the First Time in Many Years Jennifer Lopez Teases New Music on ‘Fallon’: ‘This Does Feel Like a Happy Era’ Patrick Stewart Cause of Death Revealed Raye, Rosalía, and Ella Langley Lead 2027 Grammy Nominees

It’s apparent his inclusive approach to music uplifts both musicians and fans alike. And it is contagious. His Radio City Music Hall opener began with a standing ovation.

“That is one thing that I love the most. #3350. These Are the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Kindles and E-Readers

Amazon's Black Friday sale kicked off today, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers. Timing your purchase is now a bigger deal than ever (so to speak), as Amazon recently raised the price of basically every Kindle by $50 or more due to the ongoing RAM crisis.

Because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save big on a few worthy Kindle alternatives. Here are your e-reader best bets in the lead-up to Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people. An upgraded version of the basic Kindle, the Paperwhite adds a larger screen, temperature-adjustable lighting, water resistance, and better battery life—and if you opt for the Signature Edition, you also get double the storage and no lock screen ads. Earlier this year, it jumped in price to $250, even before the company introduced a new model—but you can get the 2024 model for $179.99, 28% off the new list price.

If you want a great Kindle but you don't care about paying extra for more storage or getting rid of lock screen ads, the non-Signature Edition of the Kindle Paperwhite is also a great buy right now. The 2024 model has been discounted to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors.

If you don't need the bells and whistles of the Paperwhite, you can also pick up the standard Kindle. It's still a very capable device, with good lighting, 16GB of onboard storage, and the ability to hook up your Bluetooth speakers to listen to Audible audiobooks. The standard Kindle, which now retails for $150, is marked down to $119.99, making it the cheapest Kindle option. Though I think it makes more sense to spend $10 more on the Signature Edition, this is the way to go if you want the cute Matcha color.

If you like to read comics or you just appreciate looking at your book covers in full color, the 2024 Kindle Colorsoft is also at a strong 41% discount for Black Friday, bringing it down to around $170. For $10 less than the Paperwhite Signature edition, you get all the same perks (including an ad-free experience) and a color e-ink screen that's great for reading magazines, graphic novels, and manga. Color e-ink isn't for everyone, but if it's for you, the Colorsoft has the best color screen on the market. For an extra $10, the Colorsoft Kids Edition adds a case, a yearlong subscription to Kindle Kids+, and an extended warranty.

If you're looking for a combination e-reader and e-notebook, the Kindle Scribe is a great option. With a larger screen than Amazon's other e-readers, it offers all the benefits of the Paperwhite but adds support for the excellent Premium Pen stylus, allowing you to take notes in your Amazon e-books or create handwritten documents that you can later convert to text using the onboard AI tools. The 32GB black-and-white version of the Kindle Scribe is currently $349.99, while the Colorsoft version will run you $449.99. Both of these are the newest models, released in 2025.

The new Kindle Scribe Colorsoft has all the same great features of the black-and-white version discussed above, but adds a full-color e-ink display. Combined with the large 11-inch screen, this makes it a great device for reading comics or magazine articles as they were meant to be read, or marking up PDFs using the included Premium Pen. This device usually costs a hefty $630, but the current Black Friday sale cuts $180 off of that price.

If you want to step outside of the Amazon ecosystem, the Kobo Libra Colour is a good bet. Discounted $30 to $229.99 at Best Buy, it's currently pricier than the Kindle Colorsoft, but you get a bit more for your money. While most of the specs are similar (they both use the same Kaleido 3 screen and offer 32GB of storage), the Kobo supports a stylus, so you can jot down notes in your books or keep a digital journal. It also has physical page-turn buttons, which the Colorsoft lacks.

If you don't want to be tied to the Amazon ecosystem and/or you're looking for a device that's a bit more portable, consider the Viwoods AiPaper Reader, currently marked down to $200, its lowest price ever. It's got a 6.13-inch screen, so it's the same size and shape as your phone, and it has a crisp e-ink screen with a strong (if not temperature-adjustable) front light and 128GB of onboard storage. The best part is, it runs on an open Android system, so you can install multiple reading apps, including Kindle, Nook, Kobo, and Libby, and keep all of your books in one place. (Check out my review of the Viwoods AiPaper Reader for more—it's a nifty little device.)

If you don't have a large Kindle library, you're moderately tech-savvy, and you praise portability above all else, I can't recommend Xteink's line of e-readers more highly. The 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic is at its lowest price ever, coming in at just under $55, around $34 off the list price. Meanwhile, the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 is about a dollar more; that's a less-generous 19% discount. I own both, and while the Classic is definitely worth the current sale price, I actually prefer the form factor of the smaller X3 (currently $55.72), which is about the size of a library card.

If you're feeling tentative about trusting a seemingly no-name Chinese tech brand, read more about the devices in my review, or listen to the collected wisdom of the tens of thousands of people in the bustling r/xteink Reddit group.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3348. What China Gets From Its AI Honeypots and Smuggled Chips

You could start casting the movie right now: Jensen Huang, the Taiwanese-American CEO of Nvidia, the most important tech company in the world, is sucked into an illicit affair with a Chinese spy. The most valuable tech in the world — Huang’s super-powered computer chips — are smuggled into China or installed into data centers connected to America’s greatest rival. Above it all, the possibility of a super-intelligent AI, a true artificial mind, looms — and its creator will be positioned to rule the world.

At least, that’s the simple version of the story. But the real picture of the great geopolitical AI race is both more complex and more unbelievable than the tale of spies and smuggling that’s playing out in the press right now. China wants the U.S.’s chips — that much is clear. But why? And what can our only real rival power actually do with them? To answer this, Rolling Stone spoke with two experts in the Chinese tech sector, who pulled back the curtain on what the superpower actually wants when it comes to AI — and why it’s willing to use sex, smuggling and lies to get there.

Broadly speaking, there are two ways to think about AI, says Kyle Chan, an expert on Chinese technology development at the Brookings Institution.

The first is as a straight race to one goal: creating a truly intelligent AI that surpasses human intelligence in all general tasks and can improve itself autonomously. In the industry, this is known as AGI, or Artificial General Intelligence. This point of view holds that the first country or company to achieve true AGI will have an earth-shattering advantage over any competition in economics, war, medicine, and technology. Basically, it sets the world of AI up as a winner-take-all race. Many U.S. officials — including, at times, Trump himself — have made this argument, alongside many of the private sector CEOs actually working on the technology.

“If you start with that assumption, then the effort to slow down China is nearly existential,” Chan says. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

The biggest advantage the U.S. has is Nvidia’s chips. The most powerful computer chips in the world are made by one facility in Taiwan, using incredibly complex and rare machines manufactured by one company in the Netherlands. It is a process so detailed and scientifically complex that it might as well be magic. Other companies can make chips, of course, but none of them can make chips as well as the single manufacturing company in Taiwan that Nvidia and most of the U.S. tech giants use. AI companies need these chips, and these chips alone, to run the most advanced AI models — which is why the U.S. has done a lot to limit China’s access to them, setting export controls on who Nvidia can sell their chips to and which countries they can be shipped into.

Because of this constraint, the Chinese don’t really see AI the same way as most of the U.S. industry does.

Instead of an existential threat, Chan says, the second way to look at AI is a very powerful technology that will not necessarily lead to some massive strategic advantage for the first team past the AGI post. That makes the AI race a longer-term game, decided more by which power can holistically incorporate the advances of super-computing into its society and economy, which China has largely focused on doing

“What we’re kind of seeing unfold in the future is two different markets,” said Kenton Thibaut, a China expert at the Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab. The U.S. is focused on “frontier” systems — the absolute cutting-edge AI, powered by their chip advantage — while China is supplying “near frontier” technology that hits different parts of the market for AI technology. In China, Thibaut said, AI is viewed as a “general purpose” technology that should be harnessed for practical use as quickly as possible, rather than a more conceptual race to the furthest frontier.  Related Content Man Found Guilty of Igniting Blaze That Became the Devastating Palisades Fire Trump Says He ‘Can’t Speak To’ Whether Russia is a Friend to America Trump Got Played by Putin and Xi Your Favorite THC Drinks Are About to Be Illegal

“All of the [Chinese] policies and major policy pronouncements and planning around AI have to do with ‘How do we make this useful in society?’” Thibaut said. “I haven’t seen anything like that in the US.”

“[China’s] version of winning is being able to benefit the most from AI,” Chan says. “Integrate it in their economy, automate their factories, speed up drug discovery, et cetera. [They want it to] help them win across all these other domains, rather than this singular focus on achieving AGI.”

It’s a philosophical difference that is fueled by the physical constraints that the Chinese tech sector faces. The U.S. has access to more computing power than any other nation, allowing them to push the envelope. Companies like Anthropic have asked the U.S. government to regulate them more, fearful that their AI models will run out of control. In China, these discussions are scarce, Thibaut says, because the hardware they’re working with basically makes them moot — and the Chinese government is predisposed to prevent any societal disruptions. Instead, Chinese AI firms are usually focused on doing more with less — creating working, practical products and applications of AI that get the most out of whatever computing power they can harness.

And in some cases, that’s where the spies come in. The Nvidia honeypot scandal was largely controversial because it included a woman who ran a Singaporean front company that set up data centers in Southeast Asia stocked with Taiwan-made super-chips, and then leased the use of those chips to Chinese companies. Chan refers to this loophole, and the broader Chinese project of getting their hands on American tech, as a “bridge” to the country’s real goal: separating themselves from the Western “tech stack,” while still retaining competitive computing power. Eventually, Chan says, China wants to have its own version of the super-manufacturers in Taiwan, its own version of the very best chips — but until then, it has to use more subtle methods to get what it wants.

“If they want to keep pace today, they do still need access to Nvidia chips now,” Chan says.  Trending Stories Patrick Stewart Cause of Death Revealed Selena Gomez Shares Her Reaction to Martin Short Ruining Her Wedding Cake ‘Yes, Dear’ Star Anthony Clark's Cause of Death Revealed Marlon Jackson Reveals Stage 4 Prostate Cancer Diagnosis

Some parts of the U.S. government may be helping them achieve that. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnik had been very lax with Nvidia and Huang personally, allowing the company to continue selling to companies that the U.S. knew were linked with China. While Trump has said he views AI as a winner-take-all race, Reuters reported that his administration also signed off on the sale of 900,000 AI chips to Chinese companies in one six-month period, and his own AI Czar David Sacks has explicitly advocated for selling more chips directly to China.

China, then, has allies to go along with its spies — and it seems that one way or another, it’s getting all the chips it needs.

#3347. If You Loved 'Phony,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Our relationships are foundational to our lives—our sense of safety and how we understand the world around us. When someone close to us suddenly, imperceptibly shifts, it can be unsettling, especially because you can’t be sure what’s changed or why. Those are the waters where Hulu’s Phony swims, delivering a perfectly pitched dramedy about a teenager (Sam Nivola) who emerges from a brief coma convinced that his mother (a pitch-perfect Connie Britton) has been replaced with a double. If you loved the series (and similar shows) and you’re looking for more intriguing stories about doubles and impostors close to home, you should definitely watch Goodnight Mommy.

Goodnight Mommy definitely leans into the psychological horror aspect of an impostor mother much, much harder than Phony, but it’s just a deeper dive into the show’s darker implications (and, fair warning, this movie is dark).

A woman identified only as Mother returns from having cosmetic surgery with her face totally enveloped in bandages, and her twin sons observe strange differences in her behavior that convince them she isn’t their real mother—she appears to ignore one of her sons completely, and disciplines them much more harshly than before. The boys also find clues that bolster their fears, including a photograph showing their mother posing with a woman dressed identically to her.

The boys’ attempts to force her to confess rapidly descend into a kind of madness, ultimately leading them to tie her to the bed in an effort to force her to admit she’s not their real mother. It all leads to a reveal as affecting as Phony’s ultimate explanation (albeit a lot more grim and violent). The film goes way harder than the series, but if you were totally into the premise, this is the more horrifying version you’ll want to see. The original film is German; there was a 2022 remake starring Naomi Watts, and while it's pretty good, the original is the right choice. Stream Goodnight Mommy on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more impostor stories that dig into the psychological and emotional impact of suspecting someone has been replaced? Here are a few more movies that dig into the concept.

The Hole in the Ground offers an inversion: A mother who becomes convinced that her son has been replaced by an impostor. Firmly in the supernatural horror genre, the story still plays the same game with the viewer: Is Sarah (Seána Kerslake) crazy, or has her son, Chris (James Quinn Markey), been replaced by a creature living in the woods near their home? It’s got the same disturbing energy as Sarah struggles with how much her son’s changed behavior is her own psychological projection and how much is clear evidence that he’s no longer the same person—or, possibly, even the same species. Stream The Hole in the Ground on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

Taking a slightly more literary approach (it’s based on a novella by Fyodor Dostoyevsky), The Double explores what happens if you find yourself replaced by a doppelgänger. Simon (Jesse Eisenberg) is a nonentity—ignored at work, lonely, and silently longing for the girl living across the street, Hannah (Mia Wasikowska). One day, a new employee named James appears at Simon’s job—and James looks exactly like Simon. But James is assertive, confident, and charming, sending Simon into a spiral. As the two versions slide into a battle for dominance, Simon finds himself turning to increasingly deranged moves to rid himself of the new and improved version of himself. If you loved the psychological implications that Phony explores, check out The Double. Stream The Double on Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

On one level, Denis Villeneuve’s 2013 film is about a college professor named Adam (Jake Gyllenhaal) who discovers an actor named Anthony who looks exactly like him (also played by Gyllenhaal). When he tracks his double down, their lives merge in messy ways, ending in tragedy and one of the most striking (and confusing) final shots in cinema history. On another level, Enemy is a deft trick, exploring someone’s subconscious using dream logic and misdirection. If the best part about Phony was the disorienting sense that a secret just under the surface will explain everything, Enemy is the perfect choice. Stream Enemy on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for a deeper, crazier, and more terrifying story about doubles, Andrzej Żuławski’s 1981 film is a terrific choice. Inspired in part by his own feelings in the wake of a painful divorce, the story follows Mark (Sam Neil), a spy who returns to West Berlin at the height of the Cold War only to find out his wife, Anna (Isabelle Adjani), has been having an affair and wants a divorce. But Anna’s behavior becomes increasingly strange, and then Mark meets their son’s teacher, Helen, who looks just like Anna. And that’s before Anna kind of ... grows a replacement Mark from a tentacled creature kept in her bathroom (and that’s just the beginning of how weird this movie gets), resulting in two doubles. How much of the film is meant literally and how much simply represents the trauma of romantic betrayal and divorce is up to you, but Possession will definitely leave a mark. Stream Possession on Shudder, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Obsession looks at the Doppelgänger Effect from a different perspective. Cliff Robertson plays Michael Courtland, a wealthy businessman whose wife (Geneviève Bujold) and young daughter, Amy (Wanda Blackman), are kidnapped in 1959. When he follows police advice against delivering the ransom, both appear to be killed in an explosion. Courtland spends the next 16 years hating himself, until he encounters a young woman, Sandra (also Bujold), who looks almost exactly like his late wife. He works to make Sandra look as much like his wife as possible, and eventually proposes—but then Sandra is kidnapped in precisely the same way as his wife and daughter sixteen years before. This all leads to a head-spinning series of reveals and a twist that echoes the Hitchcock classic Vertigo. Rent Obsession on Prime Video.

#3346. Apple among the companies facing pressure from US senators over ‘nudify’ apps [U: Apple, TTP respond]

The Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps. Here are the details.

Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable users to generate nonconsensual nude images.

According to the updated rules, apps that allow users to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.

Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice.

While definitely well-intended, Apple’s changes came amid growing reports of AI-powered nudify apps, which easily allow users to generate nonconsensual intimate images.

Two months before these changes, Apple removed an app that allowed users to create pornographic deepfakes of real people after WIRED reached out for comment, which in turn came one month after San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu demanded that Apple and Google remove several nudify apps from their app stores.

Apple also removed several apps following investigations by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), which published reports in January and April revealing that such apps were widely available on the App Store, sometimes even appearing in sponsored search results.

Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports.

Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above.

Which brings us to today’s report from The Guardian.

According to The Guardian’s exclusive report, “three Senate Democrats sent letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms.”

A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of New Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion.

Commenting on the letter, both Google and Meta said they prohibit such apps or their promotion and work to detect and remove violations from their platforms, broadly echoing what Apple has repeatedly stated when reached for comment in the past over these same issues.

However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them.

Keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, said that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he added.

In its latest investigation, published just last month, TTP found 135 apps capable of generating nude or pornographic imagery on the App Store and the Play Store, using accounts registered to 13-year-old boys.

Additionally, researchers found that even accounts configured with parental controls were able to download these apps without requiring parental approval.

Despite Apple and Google removing the apps identified in the investigation, The Guardian noted that these apps continued to work on devices where they had already been installed.

Now, Senator Wyden warns that Congress may need to step in if the companies fail to do a better job of cracking down on these apps.

To read The Guardian’s full report, follow this link.

Update, 8:40 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said:

“We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for users. A number of the apps in the TTP report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities. We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process — a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch. We previously removed 28 of the apps referenced in this report before it was shared with us and have taken action on the remaining apps found to violate our rules. The report also relies on testing from older software that does not reflect current Apple safety features, including expanded protections for teens and parental controls in Screen Time that give families the ability to block kids and teens from downloading apps rated above their age.”

Expanding on the safety features mentioned in its statement, Apple noted that teens aged 13 through 17 now have certain protections enabled by default, including web content filters, even if their parents haven’t configured any restrictions, and pointed to ⁠this support article for more information.

The company added that children under 13 are required to use Child Accounts, and that the report relied on its previous 17+ age rating system, which was replaced last year with a more granular system that includes 13+, 16+, and 18+ ratings.

Just curious. Why doesn't someone from Apple try out the app before approving it, rather than approving it and waiting until people complain? I know there are many thousands of apps on the App store. But given that Apple makes money off most of these apps, it could surely afford to hire a staff charged with reviewing submitted apps to ensure compliance with the App store's guidelines and requirements before making them available in the App store. What am I missing here?

Apple also noted that in its report, TTP counted apps depicting people in swimwear or lingerie, which the company said does not constitute nudification or, in itself, violate its guidelines.

As for parental controls, Apple explained that, although apps that exceed a child’s configured age restrictions won’t appear in curated App Store sections, they can still be found through search, allowing children to request permission to download them through Ask to Buy. Without parental approval, the download remains blocked.

Apple added that Ask to Buy is supposed to require parental approval even for purchases made using gift card balances, including subscriptions. The company said that if a purchase didn’t trigger an approval request, that would be unexpected behavior, and that it is investigating further.

Update, November 19, 4:00 p.m. ET: In response to Apple’s statement, TTP director Katie Paul reached out to 9to5Mac with the following comment:

Apple’s statement on nudify apps sidesteps important issues and leaves out key context. The company says it prohibits nudify apps but doesn’t address how its age rating system for apps contributes to the problem. TTP has shown how Apple relies on information provided by app developers to set age ratings—a self-reporting system that allows many nudify and pornographic apps to be misleadingly labeled a suitable for minors. Apple also continues to talk about removing nudify apps from the App Store, without mentioning that apps that are “removed” continue to be fully functional on people’s phones.

There are many questions about Apple’s policy on nudify apps that the statement fails to address. Apple has adopted a limited definition of “nudify.” The company defines nudify apps as capable of showing someone naked, not stripping them down to a bikini or lingerie. But the company also says it bans “creepy” and “nonconsensual intimate imagery.” What if an app is used to depict a woman in a bikini without her consent? We have asked Apple to clarify that and have not heard back.

As for Apple’s comment that TTP relied on “older software,” that may refer to the fact that Apple rolled out new child safety features in the fall. Our research was conducted in summer 2026. But many of Apple’s new features pertain to parent-supervised accounts on Apple, which have to be set up by a parent. Apple relies entirely on parents to go out of their way to locate and enable these settings. This raises obvious questions about how many people actually do this.

#3345. Instagram finally lets users edit Stories after publishing, but there’s a catch

Every once in a while, Instagram rolls out an update that addresses one of its users’ most longstanding requests. Today is one of those days.

As spotted by The Verge, Instagram head Adam Mosseri confirmed today that the app will finally let users edit a Story after publishing.

This means users will be able to add stickers and drawings, fix typos or adjust text, and even change the music without having to delete the Story and publish it again, which would mean losing any views it had already received.

The catch is that users will only have 15 minutes after publishing a Story to make changes by tapping the ellipsis button at the bottom of the screen, and then selecting “Edit story.”

Here’s Mosseri’s post announcing the news:

Today’s update is the latest in a series of changes Instagram has made this year to address longstanding user requests.

Back in March, the app introduced the ability to reorder photos and videos in a carousel after publishing. In April, it added an option to edit comments (also within 15 minutes of posting), and in June, it began letting users manually rearrange posts on their profile grid.

More recently, Instagram also brought its free Edits video editor to the Mac, with multi-track editing, advanced color grading tools, and 4K exports.

#3344. This Apple Watch Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, currently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and users who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

The SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

It comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple says the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

The majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

If your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

#3342. Zane Lowe shares Apple Music Radio audience numbers, recalls ‘crickets’ in the early days

In a new interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month. Here are the details.

Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue said Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.

Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, however, has now offered a more concrete figure, revealing that the service reaches over 50 million unique listeners every month:

We were never, you know, delusional enough to assume we were going to get a huge audience overnight. We’d have to build it like anyone else would have to build anything. But we’ve just got to a point in our 11 years on where we now, overall, reach over 50 million unique listeners a month, which is a really large number for us, and it’s growing exponentially and really fast.

The revelation came in a wide-ranging interview published today with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, where Lowe discussed Apple Music Radio’s early struggles, its approach to supporting emerging artists, and why human curation remains central to the service.

When discussing the early days at Apple Music, Lowe recalled:

When we started the radio here, I didn’t have access or opportunity with a lot of the artists that I built relationships with from the BBC because we were unproven. And I came over here thinking, “Well, I’ve got Jimmy Iovine over here, and I’ve got Apple over here and I feel unstoppable, and who’s not going to want to come and launch this thing with us?” But it was kind of crickets… As upsetting as that was at the time, two good things came out of it. Number one, it snapped me back into the reality force field of building something from scratch. And number two, it made us focus really clearly and in a big way on new and emerging artists.

He also mentioned some of the first artists Apple Music Radio supported, including Billie Eilish with “Ocean Eyes,” Khalid with American Teen, and Bryson Tiller with his first song.

At the time, Lowe noted, these artists were just getting started, and supporting emerging talent became a defining part of Apple Music Radio’s approach, one that continues to this day:

The really cool number is on our radio network. We played — this year alone — over 6,500 individual artists, which is not a commercial radio model. [Other radio networks’] playlists are very small, and the amount of plays is very great. Our playlist is gigantic. We play a lot of different artists, and over half of those 6,500 artists we’ve played in one year are new or emerging. So, think about 3,300 artists, roughly, getting played, who may be on their first song, their first EP, their first album…It’s proof of concept. It’s great.

Still on the subject of the early days at Apple Music, Lowe said “it was very clear [from the start] that that was very important to everybody who was responsible for bringing Apple Music to life,” adding that “serving artists and the artistic community in a way that is of most value and of most service” still drives “a lot of the decision-making” at the platform.

When the conversation turned to Apple Music’s recent rebranding, which introduced a new logo physically created using sound waves from a composition by Fred again.., Lowe said he couldn’t speak to the decisions behind it, but stressed the human element and the creative process that went into it:

We could have created that in a way that could utilize all of the tech available. We could type that into a prompt. But at the end of the day, seeing how it’s made is so much more additionally inspiring than just seeing it. It speaks to, I think, what we try to do here, which is, we love the process of what we do, and the result is a byproduct of getting to do it and loving to do it.

The issue of algorithms also came up when Lowe discussed Apple Music’s approach to music discovery, with the executive emphasizing the importance of human curation over automated recommendations:

Well, we don’t want to say that too loudly, because someone could be like, “Wait a minute, we could cut costs here? Man, how did we not think of that!” Look, I mean, jokes aside, we’ve been incredibly fortunate, and I’ve been incredibly fortunate to take that step from the BBC into a company and to work with people that value exactly what it is you’re describing: this idea of place and this experience of sharing things with each other, and how meaningful it is when someone shares a record with you and it comes with context. It’s a gift…

#3341. Why Black Friday and Cyber Monday Are Bad Days to Impulse Buy Electronics

Black Friday sales officially start Friday, November 28, and run through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before it's over.

It's Cyber Monday, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.

Some Cyber Monday deals are still live, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.

Follow our live blog to stay up-to-date on the best sales we find.

Browse our editors’ picks for a curated list of our favorite sales on laptops, fitness tech, appliances, and more.

Sales are accurate at the time of publication, but prices and inventory are always subject to change.

Not every Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal is as sweet as it seems. With electronics and tech in particular, you could be buying last year's model that has actually been on sale since the summer—and was maybe a better price a few months ago. Here’s how to avoid impulse buying a misleading Black Friday “deal” and make sure you’re getting the best bang for your buck.

When you see products like food, clothes, or home goods with a big "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" tag slapped on them, it's probably safe to take advantage of that deal. Chances are it's the same exact product you'd find on other days of the year. The same can’t be said for a TV, laptop, and other tech deals, where the product itself is constantly being upgraded.

Because tech is always evolving, and retailers want to move inventory before new models come out, electronics are especially susceptible to a practice known as "price anchoring." That's when retailers mark up prices in the weeks leading up to Black Friday, before "slashing" those prices back down, giving the appearance of a deal that isn't really a deal at all. Still, when you see that marked-up number, aka the "price anchor," you might get tricked into thinking you're saving money when you're not. There's also the false sense of urgency that gets created. It's second nature to assume that anything labeled "deal" won’t last long—even when this so-called deal price has actually been going on since the summer.

Price anchoring isn't even unique to Black Friday. The nonprofit Consumers’ Checkbook tracked prices at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022 and found that more than half the items tracked were offered at false discounts every week or almost every week. Less common, but also worth noting, is a known practice of "derivative" or retailer-exclusive models produced specifically for the holiday shopping season. These versions often feature cheaper components, fewer features, or lower specifications than their regular counterparts. A 55-inch TV from a reputable brand might look identical to the year-round model, but it could have a lower refresh rate, inferior panel technology, or fewer HDMI ports.

In the same vein, that "amazing deal" on a laptop might come with last year's processor, or a smartphone that's about to be replaced. The issue isn't that the tech is an older model, but again, it's that it probably has been at this low a price, or lower, since the summer. Alternatively, some deeply discounted electronics are refurbished units or open-box returns that have been repackaged. Again, while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, impulse buyers may not fully realize what they're buying.

The key phrasing here is impulse buying. Events like Black Friday are psychologically engineered to trigger impulse purchases. Limited-time offers, countdown clocks, and "while supplies last" warnings create artificial urgency. When you're caught up in the moment, it's easy to convince yourself you need a new tablet, smartwatch, or gaming console, even if you hadn't considered buying one before.

To avoid a low-key scam, do your research. The easiest way to tell that you’re getting the correct product is by checking the model or serial number. And with online shopping, finding and double-checking those numbers is quick and easy. In addition, don't just compare prices—compare specs. Look at processor speeds, RAM, storage capacity, screen resolution, refresh rates, and connectivity options. A $300 laptop isn't a deal if a slightly more expensive model offers significantly better performance that will last longer.

If you do see a deal that catches your eye, it could pay to wait. Cyber Monday, post-Christmas sales, and even January clearances often feature electronics deals that rival or beat Black Friday prices, all without the famous chaos and pressure. Then again, you risk more “out-of-stock” results if you wait, so the risk is up to you, depending on the popularity of the item you’re eyeing (and how badly you want it).

The bottom line: Don’t fall victim to a falsely advertised lower-quality product, and do a little research to find actually good deals ahead of time.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

#3340. The Making of My Chemical Romance’s ‘The Black Parade’

My Chemical Romance didn’t waste a minute of their way-too-abbreviated recording career, making one of rock’s last great concept albums on their third try in the studio, 2006’s The Black Parade. It was Tommy in a white belt and eyeliner, vastly expanding the band’s sonic palette beyond the punk-thrash of their first two albums. It felt like the beginning of what should have been a long, ambitious new phase of My Chem’s career, but instead, they released the underrated Danger Days: The True Lives of the Fabulous Killjoys in 2010 and broke up three years later.

Their welcome return to the road has yet to be accompanied by new music, but the band — frontman Gerard Way, lead guitarist and backing vocalist Ray Toro, rhythm guitarist Frank Iero, and bassist Mikey Way (drummer Bob Bryar left in 2010 and died in 2024) — is promising that will change soon.

Welcome to the Black Parade recently celebrated its 20th anniversary, and a new vinyl edition made a surprise Number One debut. That album’s producer, Rob Cavallo (who also worked on much of Green Day‘s discography, among many other projects) joined Rolling Stone by Zoom for an in-depth look at the making of a 21st-century rock masterpiece.

What did My Chem first play for you that got you excited to be involved in this album?They were interviewing other guys as well, but I’ll never forget, ’cause it was so freezing cold in New York, and we went to SIR, and they played me a few things. But the one that blew my mind was “Mama.” When I heard that, I remember just jumping off the couch just going, “Oh, my God, you guys. That is so great and original,” and you could tell it was part of a deeper picture of something, even though I was new to the band. It felt important to me right away that this band was existing on a higher conceptual level.

That song sounds like the Doors version of “Alabama Song.” It’s very un-punk at first, and then it kicks into the—The heavy part, right. Yeah, I kinda likened it in a weird way rhythmically to the Doors. I was also thinking of [the Rolling Stones’] “Mother’s Little Helper.” Almost like you could see the Cossacks-style Russian dancing to it. It’s like this sort of head-bopping thing that just felt very edgy, and very anti-establishment rock in a weird way. It was definitely like the we-don’t-give-a-fuck kind of rock. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

But then there was this story in there. I was like, “What is this guy going on about? What is happening here? This is heavy stuff.” So that’s why I jumped up off the couch on that song.

And of course, a lot of the record at that point had not been written. And then I got this call and they said, “Meet us at this steakhouse near SIR.” And I remember walking there and I thought my legs were gonna freeze off. And then we got in and we had the greatest dinner ever, and they said, “All right, you wanna be our producer?” I said, “Yeah, I do.” And that was it. They decided a couple hours after the first meeting.

Do you think your enthusiasm put it over the top for them? Obviously it couldn’t have hurt that you had just done American Idiot, which had similar levels of ambition.I think I was told that they liked what I said about the music, and they probably liked that I had done two records that I think stood out in their minds. Yeah, I had just done American Idiot, which was of course really big and was working, and I think they liked that. And then I think the other record they mentioned was Jawbreaker, Dear You, which is a band and an album that had an infamous history of being a dismal failure, in a way, commercially when it first came out.

But also then received its just deserts many years later, in the fact that it was now considered one of the seminal emo records of all time. And of course, we all know the history about how the band got back together and then all of a sudden on one show there were 60,000 people singing every word to every song on that record. But at the same time we also know that Kurt Cobain was, like, one of their biggest supporters — they were opening for Nirvana. So it was kinda cool. Related Content Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Drop My Chemical Romance Lawsuit, but War of Words Rages On My Chemical Romance Top the 'Billboard' 200 With 20-Year-Old Album Live Nation Defends My Chemical Romance’s Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Lookalikes: It Was 'Parody’ Watch My Chemical Romance and Lauren Tsai’s Otherworldly Short Film Featuring Billie Eilish, Phoebe Bridgers

How did My Chem define their ambitions on that first day?It wasn’t necessarily something that we actually talked about. I think Gerard [Way] had it in his mind, but a lot of it happened when we went into this place called the Paramour. The band was looking for a place where they could live and work and write.

A sort of haunted mansion, apparently.Oh, it was haunted all right. Crazy stuff was happening all the time. You could just feel the vibes of the insanity that was happening — doors closing by themselves, and probably the eeriest hallway. To this day, I still remember that hallway going down to where the bedrooms were on the top floor, and it just looked like you were in the scariest movie. And the coat of arms and the polar bear, the stuffed polar bear, all the weird stuff that was just everywhere.

And it was also kinda freezing in there. It was such an old building that we had to bring in space heaters, and so a lot of the writing actually ended up taking place over a couple of months in that particular space. And Mikey [Way] eventually, as you probably heard, he had to move out. He couldn’t take it after a while. It was just too scary.

But we had a lot of fun there, and we got a lot of the work done. So the record, I would say, was probably 90 percent written by the time, or 95 percent written by the time we got out of there and headed to the studio. With, of course, the notable exception of the song “Black Parade” itself, that has its own sort of strange and storied history.

While they’re writing in the house, where are you and what are you doing?Every day, Monday through Friday, I’d show up with my engineer, Doug McKean, and I set up some fancy microphones in this giant, crazy living room that they had. The great room in that house looked like it was, like, 1,500 square feet. And we put the band in there with a PA, like a smaller PA, so that we could record whatever the band was writing and doing. So the writing was done almost live.

Gerard liked to just sing over the band. And someone would bring in a riff and we would just start jamming and recording. And the great news is that all of those recordings actually are now available online. I think there was a big box set of these live two-track recordings that are sort of the precursor — they’re the demos that we made the album from.

Yeah, those are available to stream now.We put them on these DAT tapes. I had a special digital audio tape recorder, which was basically a tape that would be equivalent to CD quality. We would set about writing and creating and capturing these compositions, and working on the structure of them and what have you, so that we could then go into the studio, which is, of course, radically more expensive, and make the record.

Was Gerard having his night terrors at the house, and did he think they were caused by the house?You’d have to ask him if they were being caused by the house. But one thing for sure is the house had an effect on him, because it was a strangely haunted, dark place.

And he did talk about the night terrors, and he did talk about that he was going through a lot of things at that particular time. I think he was, like, a young man at the cusp at that time. I didn’t know where he was with his significant-other situation. There might have been something going on there. I don’t really know. But I would say this, I could tell he had a great record in him.

They’re a very emotional band, and they’re the nicest people. They’re very cordial to each other, and everything is on the up and up. But they also kinda would wear their hearts on their sleeves; if they were upset about something else in life, you could hear about it, you know? I was there to be very supportive. But the one thing for sure is that nothing ever got in the way of the music. We went to work. It was serious. We seriously worked 10, 12 hours a day.

When Mikey has to leave because it’s psychologically oppressive, does it make anyone else wonder, “Hey, maybe we should get the hell out of here too?”I think there was some conversation about it, but I also think, certainly, there were financial considerations. I think that there was a lease that we had to let expire, and, like, where were they gonna stay if they go, and what other money is that? ‘Cause we were responsible and [we were] on a budget.

And you’re writing all this great stuff, so why not stay?That’s the other thing. The vibe in the daytime and into the evening, in terms of getting work done, it was working. You’re really correct on that.

So you go in the studio. Let’s talk about “Welcome to the Black Parade,” which started as “The Five of Us Are Dying.”So what was interesting is that it was a song that we thought was good, and we knew we were gonna put it on the record.

But there [were] two things about it that kinda didn’t work. One was, I remember there was, “What’s the intro gonna be?” And “Do we just pop into the song?” And it never felt totally settled. And then the other thing was the chords on the chorus were… If you listen to “Five of Us Are Dying,” you’ll see that the chord structure was slightly different, and it didn’t feel like a hit record. It just felt like an OK song.

So what happened?I really gotta give credit to Gerard and the band. So I, for whatever reason, one day showed up to the studio early. And nobody was around, and we were at the Eldorado Studio in Burbank. And so I would sometimes sit there and just play the piano in the morning and just get my ears opened up and refreshed or whatever.

And lo and behold, Gerard shows up five minutes later. We were a good half an hour, 40 minutes before everybody. And so I’m just playing the piano, and he liked that ’cause I could play Queen songs and whatever. I remember him pointing at me once when we were up at the Paramour mansion, and I started playing things. He goes, “Oh, hey, listen to Cavallo. He can actually do shit on the piano. We should use that.”

So now here we are, like a month or two later, and we’re at Eldorado. And he goes to me, “Can you play…” And he cited the graduation theme, like “Pomp and Circumstance.” He goes, “But can you do that, but just make it go down?” And so I had one of those weird moments where I said to myself, “Don’t think, just play.” And my fingers literally started playing, and Gerard almost immediately started singing, “When I was a young boy…” And it was really a magical thing, and we had a little voice note recorder or voice memo thingy, and we recorded it, and he goes, “OK, so this is the parade.” We were thinking of it as being, like, an interstitial moment in the record where you would hear a parade from half a mile away or a quarter mile away, and it’d start very light.

That’s why I played it with one finger at first. And then I started playing it with two hands, and then I started playing it as big as I could make it — loud. And then, now that the parade has passed you, it gets quieter again, right? So I worked it all the way back up to just the single-note thing, right? And the thing probably lasted two, two and a half minutes. And so then the idea was, OK, we’re gonna have marching bands, and we’re gonna have orchestral percussion and the horns and the whole thing.

But I went away with my family for a few days, and when I got back on Monday, Gerard says, “You gotta hear this. You gotta hear this.” And what they had done was they had taken the first half of “The Black Parade” and attached it to what would become the extended intro to [“The Five of Us Are Dying”]. And I was like, “Oh, my God, that totally works.”

What else did they change?I think Ray [Toro] or somebody fixed the chords on the chorus. The chorus became much more sing-along. And then all of a sudden that made sense. But what it really also did was, because we had a marching band and giant orchestrations in the intro, it afforded us the ability for me as a producer to say, “Now I can afford to have all these big orchestrations and all those things during the body of the song,” which normally you wouldn’t have a reason to do. It raised the bar of the song creatively to such a level that we could do something that in a weird way maybe on a pop-punk record had not been done before.

I remember I played it for one of my great mentors, Lenny Waronker, who was the longtime president of Warner’s, famous dude, and he went, “Holy shit. What the hell is that? I’ve never heard anything like that.” It actually worked, you know? So I remember thinking, “Wow, Lenny likes it. Yay.”

Let’s talk about “Teenagers.”He really did mean what he was saying, but sometimes an artist can do what they would call a throwaway. Because he was concerned with — this is when Columbine happened, and kids were getting violent. And that song almost didn’t make the record.

What happened was there were some people that thought, “This is like an old-school rock & roll song.” And the argument was, “Why are we doing an old rock & roll song?” Like what they call a I-IV-V [chord-progression] song, like Chuck Berry. But what’s great about that is that my argument was, how do you write a contemporary I-IV-V song that is so great? And have the lyric be that meaningful? To me, that was the argument to do it. Right?

It’s just an important record. And to be fair, it worked out, you know? Everybody agreed. It took a week or two. It was definitely a conversation, ’cause if you do listen to the record, I admit that it is an outlier on the album.

But there was just something so compelling about that. At the beginning, it wasn’t obvious even how to cut it, but we did. I remember we all took turns at, “What should the bass be like?” You know? And I think Ray actually kinda figured it out. But anyway, the point is that the record came out and look what happened. It just exploded.

I believe it was your phone call that got Liza Minnelli on “Mama.”Yeah, so we were talking about, on “Mama,” who should play Mother War? The idea of this was like Mother War is this weird character. And there was a wonderful lady — Liz Rosenberg, Madonna’s publicist. And so I was kicking around Warner’s, like, does anybody know Liza Minnelli? I think it was Gerard’s idea. It was definitely the band’s idea. And I said, “Let me see if I can get it.” So I called Liz Rosenberg and she said, “I can do it. I think I can get her.” And anyways, the fucking miracles, she did it. She got her.

What was working with Liza like?One of the things that was so great about Liza is that she was so consummately professional that we got the takes that we wanted, and she was not done. She was like, “No, I need to keep doing this. Let me keep trying. Let me perfect this. Let me get this crying part down. Let me figure out how I can truly nail this performance.” And her attention to detail, I have to say, I was just so blown away by her.

We haven’t necessarily had a ton of great guitar solo albums this century, but this is definitely one of them. Do any memories stand out?Both Ray and Frank [Iero] are great guitar players, and they did amazing things. But the thing that always stands out is the song “Dead!” And that first solo, because what’s crazy about that solo is that that happened by accident. It was supposed to just be the chords, and we weren’t gonna actually have a solo there. The chords were, like, enough.

But Ray being as great guitar player as he is, I think we just hit record or whatever, and he had the guitar in his hand, and he just ripped that solo, actually just as like a warmup or something. And we went, “We gotta use it. We gotta use it,” and he was like, “No, no. We can’t use it. We can’t use that. That’s just…” And then we printed a rough mix of the whole thing and we kept living with it, and over the course of the next week or two, I was like, “Ray, we gotta use it. It’s too good.” And eventually he said, “OK, fuck, we’ll use the solo.” But what’s amazing is it shows you how good a player he is, because that was something that was — how do I explain it? — an off-the-cuff, unplanned solo. How good is that? That this guy could just do that without even thinking about it.

The band hung out in a house for two months writing, and then recorded at a great studio. Would it be very difficult to get all that together in the current music industry, on a major label?Yes and no. It’s funny, if you look at the budgets back then for a band like that and the way the music business is now, it’s really comparing apples and oranges, right? I don’t think that Paramour was, like, that expensive, because if it’s 15 or 20 grand a month and you do it for two months, and you’re housing like five, six, seven guys, that’s actually cheap. And also rehearsing. That’s actually kinda inexpensive if you’re thinking about it in terms of real estate. If you were to pay a rehearsal place and hotels and all that kind of stuff, it’d be a lot more.

And then we went to Eldorado, which was not an A++ expensive three-grand-a-day place. It was actually more in the middle level. Like $1,200 or so — and I think we were able to crank that album out in, tops, two and a half months. So 10 weeks or something. That was a budget-conscious record, which made sense because they were a band on their way up. The prior record did well, but it wasn’t like there was like oodles of money running around all over the place.

I was kinda known as a producer that could stay on budget. So we probably did this one in the $200,000 to $250,000 range, but that’s just a total fucking guess.

Was there any sense, working on Black Parade, that this was a band about to make just one more album and then not make one for a very long time?There was no indication during making Black Parade that it was gonna be only one more album, but there was indication near the end of Danger Days that there were feelings afoot, shall we say.

The band has said there’s a new album coming. Are you working with them now?No, I was supposed to go see them at the Hollywood Bowl, and then I got the flu, so I didn’t go. But I’ve been in contact with Ray and Mikey. I really don’t know what their plans are. When I looked at it, just the idea that there’s a new piece of vinyl — I think when a band is really good and makes really good music and there’s also a bit of a scarcity about it, right? They haven’t made music in a long time. You put out this new piece of product and the hardcore fans will buy. I actually bought one myself the other day. I was at Amoeba and I said, “You know what? I should just buy one for good luck.”

You pushed it over the top. It would’ve been Number Two if you didn’t jump in there.I bought a whole one copy at $40. It’s amazing, and they sold something like, I think, 70,000 of them or something. And I think that was just in the United States, unless that was worldwide, I don’t know. But I also know it was Number One in the U.K. But what’s interesting is those numbers are, in a weird way, like old-school, unheard-of numbers, because if you sell 70,000 at $40 list price, the gross is 2.8 million bucks.

One of Amazon’s biggest sales of the year, Black Friday and Cyber Monday, is set to start Nov. 27, but many early deals are already rolling in. To take advantage of everything the sale has to offer, you’re going to need to be a Prime Member. If you sign up for an Amazon Prime account to take advantage of the sale but decide you don’t want to pay for an ongoing membership, you’ll need to cancel your subscription before the end of your free trial.

You can cancel your Prime subscription via web browser by first logging into your Amazon account. Amazon has a Cancel Your Prime Membership button on its support page to launch the process, or you can follow the steps detailed on Amazon's page:

Hover over the Accounts & Lists menu on the top-right of the window, then select the Prime Membership option.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

Note that Amazon requires a bunch of clicks to finalize your cancellation, giving you lots of “opportunities” to change your mind.

Open the Amazon Shopping app on your mobile device.

Click the three horizontal lines on the bottom right.

On the top bar, slide all the way to the end and select Help.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

As mentioned, closing your account will immediately end your access. Amazon also offers you the option to pause your benefits and billing temporarily instead of canceling them completely. Either way, your Amazon account is still active—you simply won’t have Prime benefits.

Finally, if you have other subscriptions connected to your Prime account, those will end when your billing is up. And if you signed up for Prime through the Android mobile shopping app or the Prime Video Android app, you’ll have to go through Google Subscription to manage your membership.

You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.
