#3310. Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous

Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”

These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?THREE POSSIBLE FUTURES1. The Intelligence ExplosionAI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.2. Danger Without SuperintelligenceThe intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.3. A Useful AI FuturePowerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be ComputableThere’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.Penny Gray PhotographyObjection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design)Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.” Explore the Superintelligence Debate In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”

In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”

These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Superintelligence Delusion.”

Cal Newport is a computer science professor at Georgetown University where he is also a founding faculty member of the Center for Digital Ethics. He's the author of multiple bestselling books about human flourishing in a technological world and is the host of The Cal Newport Show podcast.

Concerns about AI are legitimate. These systems can be used to intensify surveillance, generate convincing disinformation, facilitate cyberattacks, and concentrate economic and political power. More capable systems may introduce additional risks, particularly when deployed without adequate testing or oversight.

We should not dismiss these dangers. But neither should we treat catastrophe as inevitable simply because a technology is powerful.

The answer to risk is not blind faith. It is serious evaluation, independent testing, appropriate safeguards, accountability, and governance proportionate to the potential harm. High-risk applications warrant greater scrutiny than routine uses.

I think the current transformer attention method is not the method to reach ASI. There will need to be something else that pushes it forward. From my understanding the large data corpus is really just an advanced prediction system. Something will need to come along to actually understand concepts terms and know how to reason about things.

I think there's an element of expressing our values, even in the face of technological uncertainty, that this story gets at. We can still decide as a society that this handful of companies must develop their tech on terms defined by the rest of us. They may seem powerful and they are certainly telling us they intend to be even more powerful, but that's not the same as having political power today. I like Newport's idea that everyone else's voices matter, too.

#3306. Egyptian Music Star Mohamed Mounir Gets Biopic – Doha Industry Days

The life and legacy of legendary Egyptian artist Mohamed Mounir is set to be explored in a biopic spearheaded by The Film Committee at Media City Qatar.

The Film Committee has acquired the rights to document Mounir’s life story, with partners on the project set to include a leading regional studio and other partners, which have yet to be unveiled.

The project was announced at the Film Committee’s Doha Industry Days, just hours after the Qatari body gave an update on previously announced biopic Caesar, about Syrian whistleblower Farid Al-Madhhan, announcing Taim Hasan as it star. Related Stories News 'Al Hayba' Star Taim Hasan To Play Syrian Whistleblower Farid Al-Madhhan In Neon-Backed 'Caesar' Biopic News Steven Paul Talks Up Federal Film & TV Tax Credit: "It's Going To Be Good For The World" - Industry Days Doha

Mounir’s career spans nearly five decades across music, film and television. Watch on Deadline

His 1981 breakthrough album ‘Shababeek’ established him as one of Egypt’s most distinctive artists, with his work characterized by its fusion of Nubian folk and Arabic pop with Western genres like jazz, blues, and reggae.

He is known to his fans across the Middle East and beyond as “El King” in reference to his 1998 album and play ‘El Malek Howwa El Malek’ ((The King is The King).

Also working in cinema, his some 20 credits including collaborations with late Egyptian filmmaker Youssef Chahine on films including Egyptian Story (1982) and Destiny, which played in Out of Competition in Cannes in 1997 and was then selected as Egypt’s Oscar entry.

Mounir was born into a Nubian family in a village in Southern Egypt, where he spent his early childhood. His family moved to Cairo, after the village was resettled due to the construction of the Aswan Dam in the 1960s, where his singing voice was discovered when he sang at a family gathering.

The Film Committee said the biopic will trace Mounir’s journey from his humble beginnings to becoming one of the Arab world’s most celebrated and influential artists, revealing untold details, surprises, stories and anecdotes.

“Mohamed Mounir’s music holds a special place in the lives of audiences across Egypt and the Arab world,” said Film Committee at Media City Qatar Chair Hassan Al Thawadi.

“Bringing his story to the big screen is an opportunity to celebrate his artistry, the cultural heritage his work represents and its lasting social relevance, a story that connects generations of fans across the region and has the power to resonate with audiences around the world,” he continued.

“This project also builds on our recent investment in extraordinary life stories from the region and reflects our ambition to develop a world-leading slate of biographical films that brings these stories to audiences globally.”

Alongside the feature film, plans include a behind-the-scenes documentary featuring interviews with Mounir and those who have lived and worked alongside him, as well as documenting the development and production of the biopic.

With development in the early stages, the hunt is now on for an actor to play Mounir.

#3305. This Note-Taking Pebble Ring Is so Simple, and I Love It

Pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos. That seems like it would be underwhelming, and the idea was ridiculed by some of Pebble’s fans when the product was first announced. But I’ve been wearing it for a few weeks, and folks: I love it.

In this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity. This is a ring with no heart rate sensors or even charging pins, just a microphone, a button to activate it, and a light to let you know that it’s working. The audio is processed on your device; no need to send anything to the cloud.

To buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone. I use an iPhone rather than an Android, which means I can’t use certain features like setting timed reminders or connecting to Beeper, but it’s still an incredibly useful little device. The Index has no charger, since it uses a disposable battery that Pebble estimates will last about two years.

The simplest way to use the Index is to wear it on your index finger (hence the name, get it?) and press the button with your thumb. Speak a quick note while holding the button in, and the ring will flash to let you know it got the message. A moment later, you’ll get a notification saying that it added (whatever you said) to your “Notes to self” note.

To take this further, you can create different notes and ask the ring to add what you say to a specific note. You can also double-click the button to ask a question. The answer will appear in the notification you get on your phone or watch a moment later. (The ring does not speak to you.)

All the notes you leave yourself appear as plain text in the Pebble app, fully editable. If you tap on each one, you can see a timestamp from when you left the note, and you can replay the voice recording if the transcription doesn’t make sense. (Why is there a “pencil sharp pepper” on my packing list? Ohh, that’s a pencil sharpener.) You can also add notes by typing them, which I find useful when starting a to-do list or a packing list.

It’s incredible how useful a simple timestamped note can be. I used to do something similar with my “notes to self” chat in Signal, but the Index makes it even easier since I won’t get distracted by opening my phone. For example, I make a note on the Index whenever I take a medication, so that tomorrow morning I will be able to check whether I already took, say, a long-acting allergy pill. (You do not want to accidentally double up on those.)

There’s one thing that, for years, I wished for a simple tool to help me do. It’s trivial, which makes it extra frustrating that I have not been able to find a good solution. I would simply like to note when I leave for a road trip, and when I start and end each stop. This way I can tell how long the driving took as a portion of the whole trip, and how long my stops tend to be so I can plan them better next time.

You’d think this would be easy, but every existing tool drove me nuts in a different way. Stopwatches only store a single number, so I can’t break down how long each stop was—and if I miss a button press, I’m screwed. Sending myself a Signal text is probably my best option, but if I’ve just parked my car after three hours of driving, the second I pick up my phone I’m going to see all the notifications that arrived while I was on the road, and I’ll forget to actually send that text.

But this is exactly what the Index does well. I don’t even need to open my phone or look at my watch. Pressing the button with my thumb means I can do this one-handed without having a microphone always listening. (It’s also a great way to jot down the random things I think of while driving.)

The Index worked perfectly for my travel log, and I even used it for a workout after I got to my hotel room that night. I’d do 10 pushups, then tell the ring “add 10 pushups to my workout.” I’d do 20 crunches, and add that as well. I left the workout note open on my phone and could glance over and see what I had already done, since my messages got added to the note as I went.

I didn’t need a workout app for any of this, or a special-purpose travel app. I can just leave myself a dang note, and the note-taking app can remember when I left the note and, if I choose, play back exactly how I said it. It’s gloriously simple. Good job, Pebble.

#3304. UK court rules Apple can share the top secret order everyone already knew

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal – essentially a British court that deals with complaints about state surveillance – has ruled that Apple is allowed to reveal a secret order it received from the UK government.

Apple had already found a clever way to alert British customers to the classified order without breaking the law, but it can now confirm what we all already knew, and talk openly about the issue …

In 2025, the British government ordered Apple to create a backdoor to allow access by security services and law enforcement. Even worse, the order was issued under legislation that prohibits companies from revealing that they have received this demand.

This would have meant that British customers who enabled ADP would think that their data was safe when in fact it wasn’t. As we’ve said many times before, any backdoor created for use by the good guys is vulnerable to discovery and exploitation by the bad guys.

“Apple can no longer offer Advanced Data Protection (ADP) in the United Kingdom to new users and current UK users will eventually need to disable this security feature. ADP protects iCloud data with end-to-end encryption, which means the data can only be decrypted by the user who owns it, and only on their trusted devices. We are gravely disappointed that the protections provided by ADP will not be available to our customers in the UK […] As we have said many times before, we have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products or services and we never will.”

Tell me you’ve been ordered to create a backdoor to ADP without telling me you’ve been ordered to create a backdoor to ADP …

The UK government must admit that it issued a secret order to Apple to allow it access to encrypted customer data, a court has ruled […] The Home Office has “not established that it would be damaging to national security” to reveal that Apple had received a “technical capability notice” (TCN), the tribunal said. The ruling means that […] “much” of Apple and the non-profits’ legal challenge can now take place in open court.

One of the great ironies is that most people had never heard of ADP until the government effectively made it headline news in the tech press three years after it launched – a classic example of the Streisand Effect.

This ruling is a win both for transparency and commonsense. To be clear, the actual requirement for a backdoor remains in place, but this can now be challenged in open court.

#3302. Gemini Notebook's New Interactive Site Builder Is Much More Useful Than I Expected

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

Gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses. Now there's something new. You can also build interactive websites from your notebooks.

That might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code. But it gives you another way to look at your material and to get insights from it. Here's how it works, what you could potentially do with it, and how impressively it worked when I put it to the test on some early 20th-century Irish literature.

Website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all users, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app.  You won't see a website option in the Studio panel alongside Audio Overview, Reports, Quiz, and the rest; instead, you type something along the lines of "make me a website" in the prompt box.

To make a website, you need sources, so I set Gemini Notebook to collect information about James Joyce's 1914 collection of short stories, Dubliners. As I studied Dubliners many years ago (I highly recommend it), I was hoping I'd spot any AI errors and hallucinations, and be able to properly assess the quality of Gemini Notebook's analysis.

With a suitable amount of information absorbed into the AI brain, I got Gemini Notebook to make me a website. Google doesn't give too much official guidance here, but says you should add "a description of what you want to build for work or study," so if you have a particular style or angle in mind, include it.

Here was my prompt: "Build a website using all the sources and information collected so far. Make it an interactive guide to the individual stories in Dubliners, as well as the overarching themes and context. I want to use it as a study aid to explore different aspects of the story collection."

The finished website pops up in the Studio panel, and in my case it took around five minutes to put something together from 26 different sources. Click on the website, and it opens in a new window—you can use it from there, open it in a separate tab, or download the code to your computer.

I was honestly impressed by how much Gemini Notebook managed to pack into a single website: I got plot summaries, analysis, critical context, and some of the main themes and motifs outlined. There was an interactive quiz at the bottom of the page to test my knowledge, and even a graphic I could click through to reveal different elements of how the stories fit together.

Everything was well laid out and functional, albeit with the standard "sheen" you get from anything made by AI (which tends to always pick the same colors and fonts). I wouldn't have necessarily thought that I needed a website if I was still studying Dubliners today, but I can definitely see how it would have helped.

For something like my project, a website really works well as a study aid, since it offers a different way of interrogating the information. You can already do that in the main chat, and with tools such as the audio and video overviews, but this is different. It's a bit like having a mini-Wikipedia focused just on whatever you're researching.

The interactive elements that are included—so in my example, I could click from story to story, and theme to theme, within the same page—make a site more engaging than a standard report document and a static wall of text, and should help the information stick if you're trying to study it.

I can also see how this might be useful for sharing data with others. Maybe you need to analyze monthly report figures, or you want to chart how your organization has developed a product over time—perhaps an interactive website will relay that information in a more compelling way than a slide deck or PDF.

Maybe you have a notebook stuffed with details of a big family vacation. Putting together a website through Gemini Notebook would give your family a hub that they could use to easily check up on the details of the trip—where you're going and when, what you'll see there, what they need to pack, and so on. Another idea might be a family tree, if you have ancestry data and sources packed together in a notebook. Putting together a website would be a great way to visualize it, and, again, it's something you could share with relatives. If there were updates to the data you've collected, you could generate a new website.

Bear in mind that you can do a lot with your prompt. My website turned out the way it did because that's what I asked for, and if you need more interactivity or specific types of sections, then you can ask. Based on my follow-up prompts, you can also specify colors and certain layout choices, though it's not quite a full-scale website builder.

It looks like these sites are single-page creations, though they do have interactive elements and sections that change as you click around. It might be better to think of them as mini apps rather than sites. As of yet, there's no built-in option for publishing a site online or sharing it with others, so you need to download the HTML and do that manually.

#3301. iOS 27.3 beta can cause HomeView issues, Apple confirms

Apple’s new HomeView just launched last Friday, but some early adopters reported issues with Siri AI in their first days of use. Apple shipped fixes in HomeView 27.2.1 yesterday, but it also confirmed the iOS 27.3 beta is responsible for some of the problems.

Yesterday Apple released its first post-launch software update for HomeView, less than a week after the product debuted.

Per the company’s official release notes, HomeView 27.2.1 focuses on bug fixes, including a fix for the following issue:

Pairing with an iPhone or iPad running the iOS or iPadOS 27.3 beta may cause Siri requests to fail

It’s unknown how many reports of Siri issues on HomeView can be attributed to the iOS 27.3 beta. However, it wouldn’t surprise me if many of the reports were from beta users. That’s in part because early HomeView reviewers didn’t seem to have the same problems.

With HomeView 27.2.1 now available, those problems should hopefully be taken care of. However, if you’re on the iOS 27.3 beta, there’s a new issue you’ll need to deal with temporarily.

As discovered by pdfu, if you try to make a Personal Content request on an iPhone running iOS 27.3, Siri in HomeView 27.2.1 now says: “I can’t help with that because your personal device is on newer software.”

If you’re on iOS 27.3, Siri on HomeView can’t use your iPhone for personal context, likely until December.HomeView won’t send Siri requests to an iPhone on newer software. Without a HomeView update, your only option is iOS 27.2.x.On-device requests like timers still work. https://t.co/8UbRs7z496

It’s understandable that issues might arise from having iOS and HomeView software that’s out of sync. Unfortunately though, there’s no beta software available for HomeView at the moment.

That means unless Apple releases a beta soon, users might have to wait until the public launch of HomeView 27.3 in December to get Personal Content features back.

How has Siri AI been working for you on HomeView? Let us know in the comments.

Kate Middleton is starring in her first documentary, and it’s a personal one. Heal, which will premiere on the BBC in the UK on November 29 and NBC in the U.S. on November 30, follows the Princess of Wales as she undertakes the National Three Peaks Challenge and reflects on her life as a cancer survivor.

In June, Middleton completed the National Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours to support The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity. She had a crew filming her for the documentary, the existence of which had not been revealed until now.

In Heal, set against the backdrop of the challenge, Middleton reflects on her cancer experience alongside others who have faced major health issues, discussing the impact serious illness can have on the afflicted person and those around them as well as places and experiences that can help in the healing process while exploring life beyond diagnosis and recovery. Watch on Deadline

You can watch a trailer below. It features Middleton’s brother James, who accompanied her on a climb, and her husband, Prince William, and children George, Charlotte and Louis embracing her at the end of the challenge.

In the U.S., the documentary will run at 8:00 p.m. on NBC and 11:30 p.m. on Bravo on November 30, streaming on Peacock next day. In the UK, it will air on BBC at 6:15 p.m. GMT on November 29. Additionally, Heal is set for release via NBCUniversal on Channel 9 in Australia on December 1 and CTV in Canada on December 7.

Produced by Detail Films, Heal is directed by Benji Jackson. All proceeds from the distribution of the documentary are going to the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity.

This is Middleton’s first time headlining a documentary. Prince William has done it a couple of times, tackling subjects he is passionate about with projects such as Prince William: We Can End Homelessness. He and his brother, Prince Harry, partnered on Diane, Our Mother: Her Life and Legacy almost a decade ago.

#3299. 10 Shows Like 'The Body' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Netflix's newest streaming hit, The Body, is drawing in millions of viewers, great reviews, and a gaggle of protests from people who didn't much care for the trailer. But if your lesbian-forward supernatural horror series isn't drawing cries of "blasphemy!"...what are you even doing? In that spirit, we'll conjure up some other shows dealing with the (extremely) dark side of high school.

This time-hopping survival drama is about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive—the extent of which we only learn about via flashbacks from the present day, where the events of 19 months spent in the wild continue to resonate. There are ambiguous teases of the supernatural here (much more ambiguous than in The Body), but there's plenty of human-level horror as well. The show explores the nasty things we get up to when in survival mode (whether trapped in the wilds, stuck with other teenagers—or god forbid both at once), while also cynically (but accurately) positing that there's a huge difference between the version of the past we talk about and the one that really happened. Stream Yellowjackets on Paramount+.

Situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It quickly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, and the ways in which we'll do just about anything when survival is on the line. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Juicy import Elite follows a group of working-class friends who earn scholarships to Las Encinas, a fictional private school that is, in the show’s universe, the most exclusive in Spain. What they find there is snobbery, mystery, murder, and lots and lots of sex (between and among characters of various sexual orientations and numerical groupings). The smart, wonderfully trashy show ran for a shocking (in our modern streaming era) eight seasons, with a couple of regional remakes. There's no supernatural stuff here, but plenty of dark deeds done with youthful vigor. Stream Elite on Netflix.

A teenager, Mae (Madeleine Arthur), is discovered by the side of the road with weird religious symbols carved into her skin. The hospital psychiatrist who treats her (Emily Deschanel) takes pity on, and interest in, Mae, deciding to take her in while arrangements can be made for a more permanent home for the cult escapee. Mae is, after all, level-headed and quiet, and couldn't possibly be any trouble. Hoo boy, yeah, that turns out to be a bad call on the good doctor's part. Stream Devil in Ohio on Netflix.

A different type of blasphemy at play here, in that Joan Lindsay's novel was already adapted brilliantly by Peter Weir in 1975, in a film often referred to as the greatest to come out of Australia. And yet, this Natalie Dormer-lead take is an achievement in its own right, the extended running time of a miniseries offering up more time to sit with the story's deliberately ineffable mysteries. Dormer plays Hester Appleyard, headmistress of a school for young ladies in the Australian bush. It's going well until a Valentine's Day picnic to the title's Hanging Rock sees three students and a governess disappear, impossibly, without a trace, bringing about the slow unravelling of pretty much everyone left behind. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on Prime Video and Tubi.

Mariam (Andria Tayeh) is brutally bullied by the cool clique at her private school in this Jordanian import, a high school drama that's both universal and distinctly Muslim in character. Fed up, Mariam convinces a couple of similarly outcast friends to join forces with her in a revenge plot that quickly gets out of hand. The show deals with Jordanian-style patriarchy head-on, without drawing any easy conclusions about its characters—Mariam catfishes one of her bullies and convinces her to send a revealing picture, one that she immediately posts, exploiting the very same repressive cultural elements that she claims to deplore. It's a smart, realist drama with soapy elements and nothing by way of the supernatural, but it's still a very sharp picture of the extremely cutthroat nature of high school life. Stream AlRawabi School for Girls on Netflix.

Peyton List stars as Maddie, a teenager in small-town Wisconsin for whom her death is very much just the beginning. Stuck in a high school in the afterlife (because hell is definitely for children), she goes on a journey to solve her own murder while uncovering secrets and lies in both worlds. It all sounds a bit grim, but the show has a sense of fun about it: While Maddie does develop the ability to communicate with the living, her world is populated by ghost teens from various eras and generations, with customs, mores, and cliques having developed in ghost high school just as in our world. Stream School Spirits on Paramount+.

The new Girigo app, claiming to grant wishes, sounds like harmless fun. Except, of course, that the things that teenagers want aren't always beneficent, and the app has already been the conduit for some incredibly dark deeds by the time it gets into the hands of the five high schoolers who find themselves caught in a Ring-like web of shamanistic horror and death countdowns. This is why we tell you to put your phones down once in a while... Stream If Wishes Could Kill on Netflix.

Four one-time best friends reunite at Rosewood High School a year after the disappearance of the leader of their little clique, all having received threatening messages from the mysterious "A," who knows everything they did last summer...and pretty much all the rest of the time. Shoplifting, parents having affairs, students hooking up with teachers—you name it, it's happening in town, and A knows it all. After the prime suspect turns up dead, the girls are caught in the killer's web while trying to keep their secrets hidden. If seven juicy seasons and three A's aren't enough for you, there are three spin-offs. Stream Pretty Little Liars on Hulu and HBO Max.

#3298. Microsoft To Do is retiring, including Mac and iOS apps

Microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps. Here’s what users need to know.

The last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027. That date also applies to Windows, Android, and the web. The underlying service and sync support will retire later, according to Microsoft’s support document.

“Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains. “For work or school accounts, Microsoft Planner will be the destination for managing personal work tasks alongside assigned work. The updated My tasks experience begins rolling out in December 2026.”

On the Mac, you can use Planner on the web or in Teams. Microsoft explicitly says it has no plans for a native Mac app.

You can still see your existing To Do tasks in Planner through June 30, but your tasks and lists won’t carry over. Microsoft plans to offer an export option before the apps retire.

Planner doesn’t support personal Microsoft accounts however. If that’s how you use To Do, you’ll need to pick another task manager, even if you pay for Microsoft 365 Personal or Family, according to the company.

The June shutdown will end a run of just over a decade for To Do on Apple platforms. Microsoft bought the company behind Wunderlist in 2015 and released the first iPhone preview of To Do in April 2017.

Looking for a proper replacement? Apple’s built-in Reminders app can keep lists in sync between Apple devices, including a grocery list you share with family through iCloud.

Microsoft has been trying to make Teams as the super app for some time now, as Planner is integrated into Teams. Teams is one of the prime examples of why super apps are terrible, with a bloated, web app-like experience.

If you liked To Do because it worked across platforms, Todoist has apps for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Windows, and Android.

Does this sunsetting affect you? Were you a Wunderlist user back in the day? Share your thoughts in the comments.

Update: Howard Crow, Director of Product, Agents and AI, Microsoft, shared this statement with 9to5Mac regarding the transition:

“We’re bringing task management experiences together across Microsoft 365 to make it easier for customers to manage individual tasks and team plans. As part of this transition, Microsoft To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027, with work and school experiences coming together in Microsoft Planner. Existing integrations across Microsoft 365, including Outlook and Teams, will also be updated to work with Planner. We recognize this change will affect customers differently, particularly those using personal Microsoft accounts, and we’re committed to helping them prepare. Customers will be able to export their To Do data before retirement, and we’ll share additional guidance to support the transition.”

That’s definitely the case with several top Asics shoes right now, and having tested both the latest and past models of popular picks like the Novablast, Gel-Nimbus and Gel-Kayano I can tell you what you are — and aren’t — missing out on by getting an older shoe.

The Sonicblast is not one of Asics' better-known shoes, but flying under the radar means that it's one of the most heavily-discounted right now. It's a plated trainer with a firm, fast ride that's good for workouts or races, and best paired with a more comfortable option like the Gel-Nimbus in a running shoe rotation.

The Cumulus sits below the Nimbus in the Asics line-up as a more affordable cushioned daily trainer, and I think the Gel-Nimbus 27 is better value than the Gel-NImbus 28 in the sales right now thanks to this deal. It has a smooth ride and is comfortable for long runs, and the newer Gel-Cumulus 28 isn't a major upgrade based on my testing.

The Gel-Kayano is Asics' premium stability running shoe, offering a little more support for overpronators on the run than the Gel-Nimbus 28. I've been testing the Kayano for many years and while there have been some changes made with the Asics Gel-Kayano 33, I rate the Gel-Kayano 32 the better buy thanks to this deal.

I keep hoping to see the Novablast 5 drop cheaper than this in the sales, but so far it's stuck firmly at $129, which is no doubt a sign of its popularity. I rate the Novablast as the best Asics cushioned shoe myself, because it's lighter and livelier than the Nimbus and Cumulus. While the Asics Novablast 6 is an excellent update the Novablast 5 remains a great daily trainer worth considering at this lower price.

I'm currently testing the Asics Gel-Nimbus 29, which has a very different feel to the 28 thanks to a softer midsole foam. Many will prefer the new shoe for this, but it actually strays into the 'too soft' category for me, sapping the energy at times during runs. If you don't want to take that risk, the Gel-Nimbus 28 is a reliable cushioned cruiser that's reduced by $40 in the sales.

The Asics Superblast 3 is one of the better running shoes I've tested this year, but I'd still eye up this deal on the Superblast 2 in the sales if you're looking for a versatile max-cushioned sneaker. It's great for all kinds of runs, and I often used the Superblast 2 for trips with a lot of walking as well.

#3295. iPadOS 27.3: Three new features coming to your iPad

iPadOS 27.3 is now in beta and will launch to all users next month, here are three new features it introduces for iPad.

There’s a new setting in iPadOS 27.3 that I instantly turned on and have been loving. It lets you double-tap the top of a window to resize it.

Inside Settings ⇾ Multitasking & Gestures, if ‘Windowed Apps’ is enabled there’s now a new toggle: ‘Double-tap Top of Window to Zoom.’

I’ve been using this gesture all the time in the beta, because it lets me resize my window to fullscreen then revert it to its previous size with ease. It’s an intuitive, convenient way to resize windows for different tasks.

Read more: iPadOS 27.3 adds new iPad setting I instantly turned on

Visual intelligence was available on iPad already, but iPadOS 27.3 adds a dedicated hub for using the feature: a new Siri mode in the Camera app.

iOS 27 brought Siri mode to the iPhone’s Camera app, but it was missing from iPad. iPadOS 27.3 corrects that oversight, letting you use your iPad’s built-in Camera app to ask Siri about any object you capture.

Baking visual intelligence into Camera should expose the feature to a lot more iPad users, since before you had to set up a custom control or shortcut for it. And with how much better visual intelligence has gotten thanks to Siri AI, the Siri mode is a valuable addition.

Read more: iOS 27 gives the Camera app on iPhone a brand new mode

Freeform is gaining a variety of new features in iPadOS 27.3. They’re available in macOS and iOS too, but out of all Apple platforms, Freeform feels very much built for the iPad.

Which iPadOS 27.3 features are you most looking forward to? Let us know in the comments.

#3294. ‘Vengeance Is Mine’ Director Edwin Reveals Cast For ‘Dancing With My Shadow’ Based On Generation-Defining Album

EXCLUSIVE: Indonesian filmmaker Edwin has revealed the five young leads for his upcoming feature, Dancing With My Shadow (Menari Dengan Bayangan: Evakuasi), inspired by the album of the same name from Hindia.

Produced by Palari Films, the coming-of-age drama marks a return to youth-focused stories for Edwin following horror film Sleep No More (2026), which premiered in Berlinale Special Midnight earlier this year, and darkly comic action romance Vengeance Is Mine, All Other Pay Cash, which won the Golden Leopard at Locarno film festival in 2021.

Based on the album by singer-songwriter Baskara Putra (a.k.a. Hindia), Dancing With My Shadow will star a mix of rising talent and familiar faces, including Rafly Altama, known for Riri Riza’s Rangga Cinta, and Hyori Mika, who stars in Palari Films’ recent Tokyo prize winner Jani Be Good. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Documentary Kate Middleton Documentary 'Heal' Set At BBC & NBC; Special About Princess' Three Peaks Challenge & Cancer Journey Gets Release Date & Trailer News Egyptian Music Star Mohamed Mounir Gets Biopic - Doha Industry Days

Also joining the cast is Muzakki Ramdhan, a former child actor from well-known genre films such as Gundala and Satan’s Slave 2: Communion, who already has more than 30 films under his belt.

Newer faces in the young cast include Daffa Saputra, an actor and fashion model for whom this is his first significant film role, and Freya, a member of the JKT48 idol girl group, who started her acting career in horror hit Dominion Of Darkness and family drama A Brother And 7 Siblings.

The cast is being revealed tonight at the final of the DBL Jakarta Series, Indonesia’s biggest high school basketball league, the world where the story takes place.

Released in 2019, Hindia’s Menari Dengan Bayangan became the soundtrack of a generation, touching on subjects that young Indonesians rarely talk about openly: anxieties around growing up, pressure from home, and the fear of being left behind. It holds the record as the most-streamed Indonesian-language album on Spotify, and still regularly appears on the platform’s weekly Top Albums chart in Indonesia.

The team behind the film explain that the album’s themes have been reworked into an original story, “with the music serving as an emotional map rather than a script”. Written by Winnie Benjamin, the story follows a quiet teenager, Agra, still grieving his father, who becomes the photographer for his high school’s rowdy basketball supporters club. Behind chants and chaos, he finds friendship, first love and a group of kids quietly learning how to survive.

Produced by Palari Films’ Muhammad Zaidy and Meiske Taurisia, the film will be executive produced by Baskara Putra, Mira Lesmana and Dian Sastrowardoyo, with music by Petra Sihombing and Enrico Octaviano.

Baskara will also appear in the film as himself performing on a concert stage. Commenting on the project he said: “This album feels like my own child. I’ve always wanted my albums to take on new forms, but handing it to someone else was scary. Then I realized the film shouldn’t be my life story. It should be a new story born from the same feelings. Edwin has always filmed young people honestly, without looking down on them. That’s what these songs needed.”

For Edwin, the project marks a return to youth stories a decade after 2017 coming-of-age drama Posesif, which won a Citra Award for Best Director. “Agra spends most of the film behind a camera, deciding what to frame and what to leave out. I think that’s how many of us lived our teenage years,” Edwin said. “The stands are full of noise and bodies, but everyone there is carrying something they don’t talk about. I wanted to stay close enough to feel it.”

Zaidy said: “From Posesif to Ali & Ratu Ratu Queens and Dear David, and now Menari Dengan Bayangan: Evakuasi, we keep coming back to coming-of-age stories. There’s always a fascinating crossroads in them. They feel familiar to so many people, yet there’s always a sense of liberation and empathy for people going through a transition in their lives. That stays relevant, even for adult audiences.”

Dancing With My Shadow is being lined up for an Indonesian theatrical release in summer 2027.

#3293. If You Loved 'Yellowjackets,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Yellowjackets is a vibe. The story of a high school girls’ soccer team that crashes into the wilderness and spends years fending off madness, starvation, and despair (and not always doing a very good job of any of those things) is equal parts funny and terrifying. The dual timelines build tension around the story’s many mysteries, and the complex characters (no one’s completely good or evil on this show) make for a lot of surprising plot swerves that feel grounded despite the supernatural implications all around them. If you’re looking for more of that specific flavor of horror, you should probably watch Alive.

Based on the true story of a rugby team whose plane crashed in the Andes Mountains in 1972, Alive will satisfy anyone whose favorite part of Yellowjackets is the core premise: Survivors of a disaster are stranded in the wilderness without supplies, and have to figure out how—and, er, who—they’re going to eat.

The survivors are initially as calm and resourceful as someone could be under those circumstances. They use the wrecked plane as shelter in the withering cold, they scavenge for anything that could be useful, and they ration out the only food they have: Some chocolates and a case of wine. But an early mistake leaves them without any food at all, and slowly they come to the sickening realization that their best chance at survival is to treat the corpses of their friends and families scattered around the crash site as a food source.

There’s no supernatural aspect, but the story has a similar tone of desperation and despair as Yellowjackets. These are people determined to survive in an impossible situation, and they do things that no one outside of their shared experience could possibly understand. The real-life origins of the story add a sense of horror that more than matches the fictional “It” that haunts the girls of Yellowjackets; putting yourself into that very real experience makes it clear just how terrified everyone was. Rent Alive on Prime Video.

If you’re craving more cannibals, cults, and crazies at the mercy of nature itself, here are a few more movies you should check out.

If you want to watch a movie that is essentially an adaptation of Yellowjackets, check out Eden. Even though it was released years before the show, the stories are so similar (albeit largely gender-flipped) that the producers of Eden actually sued, claiming plagiarism (they lost). In the film, a men’s soccer team (and two women on the same plane) crash-land on a deserted island, and as they fight for survival, things descend into, yes, madness and cannibalism as the survivors suffer dwindling food and water supplies and the rise of two violently opposed factions. It’s not nearly as deeply imagined as Yellowjackets, and it doesn’t have the supernatural hints of the show, but if you want a truly similar story, it’s a good choice. Stream Eden on The Roku Channel, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

You obviously cannot discuss Yellowjackets without discussing Lord of the Flies, William Golding’s 1954 novel about a group of schoolboys who descend into brutality and savagery when they’re stranded on a deserted island. The book has been adapted many times, but the 1963 version directed by Peter Brook is still the best version. Brook managed to elicit remarkably naturalistic performances from his young actors, giving the story a realistic tone that is somehow more terrifying than any amount of horror vibes. Stream Lord of the Flies on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

A slower and more haunting story, Picnic at Hanging Rock explores some of the same themes as Yellowjackets in an entirely different way. On Valentine’s Day in the year 1900, several students and teachers from an all-girls private school in Victoria, Australia, head to Hanging Rock for a picnic. Four students head off to explore and fall inexplicably asleep, and then three vanish, along with one of the teachers. Dreamy and drenched in dread, the story never offers any easy answers, and it explores themes of invading natural areas where you’re not wanted, burgeoning (and confusing) adolescent sexuality, and how our fear of the unknowable warps our perspective and often diminishes our humanity. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

You can never really go wrong with a Hitchcock film, and if you’re looking for another story about a disparate group of people forced to make terrifying decisions in order to survive, watch Lifeboat (based on a story by John Steinbeck). One of the director’s most underrated films, it’s the story of a group of survivors in a lifeboat after a German U-boat sinks their ship during World War II (including one survivor from the German boat). It’s a masterful suspense engine that’s not afraid to have its characters discuss the moral and ethical quandaries facing them as they struggle to survive and maintain their humanity under a constant threat of death. Stream Lifeboat on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

If you love the supernatural aspects of Yellowjackets as the girls come to believe a force they call “It” is out in the woods, check out The Ritual. Four friends embark on a hike in the wilds of northern Sweden to honor their deceased friend. When one of them is injured, they leave the marked trail to take a shortcut through the forest—where they are soon forced to shelter in an abandoned cabin, just like the Yellowjackets—and things begin to slide into the terrifying when they encounter a cult worshipping an ancient deity that grants them immortality in exchange for human sacrifices. It’s as if the show was condensed to an hour-and-a-half and the terror quotient was turned way, way up. Stream The Ritual on Netflix.

Ladies and gentlemen, I think we can all agree 2026 has been a console pricing onslaught. But it's not all bad — Grand Theft Auto 6 and Black Friday deals have finally rolled into town. If you want to upgrade your system alongside taking your first steps around Vice City, now's the time.

Sadly, while accessories and games are getting reduced, the console prices themselves are staying put at the time of writing. Of course, I'll update this article if that changes. Meanwhile, if you want to expand your collection with non-Rockstar titles, the annual PlayStation Black Friday sale is already live with deals from $7. For example, you can get Cyberpunk 2077 for $35.

There's a lot of time left to run on the Black Friday promotions, so we'll surely see more deals as we get closer to November 27. So, whether you’re based in the United States or the United Kingdom, here are the PS5 Black Friday deals to pay attention to.

The Sony Inzone H5 is one of the best gaming headsets to use with both PS5 and PC. Lightweight and comfortable to use for long periods of time, the H5 can last for 28 hours on a full charge. It also boasts 40mm drivers to provide detailed sound and supports 3D audio for immersive gaming.

Sony's first set of PlayStation wireless earbuds, the Pulse Explore, are discounted this Black Friday. These are a great pick if you don't want to wear a bulky over-ear headset while playing multiplayer games.

Snag the PlayStation 5's latest VR headset, the PSVR 2, for $56 off, and this bundle also throws in one of the best PSVR 2 games, Horizon Call of the Mountain, at no extra cost. The PSVR 2 brings serious high-quality gaming credentials with a 4K OLED picture at up to a 120Hz refresh rate and one of the best VR controllers around, the VR 2 Sense.

Take your PS5 gaming up a level with the DualSense Edge. The first official "pro" created by Sony, it's the most premium version of the DualSense, allowing you to fully customise your play experience. You tweak stick sensitivity and dead zones, and even remap each button individually. Plus, it includes adjustable back buttons. The DualSense Edge in a Midnight Black hue is also on sale for $169 right now. Also check: Best Buy | Walmart | PlayStation Direct

Sony’s standard PS5 pad remains one of the best controllers around thanks to its responsive haptic feedback and adaptive triggers. Standard colourways, including white, midnight black, cosmic red, and galactic purple, are down to £43 here, beating PlayStation Direct’s sale price.

Fresh off Robert Pattinson being named the new James Bond, Sony’s 007 First Light collector’s pad feels well timed. Finished with a golden sheen and gun-barrel motif framing Bond’s codename, it packs the same adaptive triggers and haptic feedback as the regular DualSense.

Available to new sign-ups or existing members upgrading their tier, Sony’s top-level subscription unlocks online multiplayer, monthly games, cloud streaming, and hundreds of PS5 and classic PlayStation titles. Just note it auto-renews at £119 fter the first year unless you cancel.

Built with planar magnetic drivers for crisp, detailed 3D audio, this over-ear headset connects to your PS5 over low-latency PlayStation Link while pairing to your phone via Bluetooth at the same time. A retractable, noise-rejecting boom mic rounds out the package.

Sony’s virtual-reality headset plugs straight into the PS5 with a single USB-C cable and includes eye tracking, headset feedback, and two Sense controllers. This bundle throws in a download code for Horizon Call of the Mountain alongside the £90 discount.

Sequel to Horizon Zero Dawn on the PS4, Horizon Forbidden West takes everything that was great about its predecessor and expands upon it. In this open-world action/adventure game, you take control of Aloy: a warrior in the post-apocalyptic United States that has been reclaimed by nature. There, she must contend with animal-like machines, as well as cunning human foes, as she ventures from her homeland towards the coast of the Pacific.

Housemarque's challenging, procedurally generated third-person roguelike shooter is still one of the PS5's best games, and if you've yet to play it, it's a bargain at this price. The game sees you taking the reins as Selene Vassos, a pilot who crash-lands on an ever-changing world home to tons of dangerous alien lifeforms. #3290. Halide camera app just got even better for iPhone Duo

Halide 3.4 is out today as the latest update to the pro camera app. The update adds several new features, including a larger viewfinder for iPhone Duo and more.

The new Halide update also lets you use the outer screen on iPhone Duo as a live preview or a fill flash. It brings back a few camera tools from Halide Mark II as well.

Lux Optics first added iPhone Duo support in October with Halide 3.3. With the phone fully open, the initial iPhone Duo update let you review your most recent photo alongside the live viewfinder.

Today’s new XL mode gives you the option to swap the photo preview for a larger viewfinder. Controls on both sides enable two-handed shooting.

While the Duo is open, the outer screen can mirror Halide’s camera controls or show a full-screen viewfinder without controls. The second option lets the person you’re photographing see how you’ve framed the shot.

In low light, Halide can use the outer screen as a fill flash. That gives you a softer source of light for portraits, and Halide’s developers recommend turning the screen brightness all the way up before taking the photo.

Halide also now places the histogram along the Duo’s crease. The update revises the Photo Lab interface for editing with the Duo half open as well.

On other iPhones, Halide 3.4 restores the color and luminance histograms and the shutter timer from Mark II.

Halide Mark III launched back in May with a redesigned camera and the new Photo Lab editor. Recent updates added RAW-only capture in 3.1 and Aperture Priority for iPhone 18 Pro in 3.2. Halide Mark III version 3.4 is available now on the App Store.
