#3258. Community-Focused Academic Brings AI Tools to Colorado Farmers

This senior member’s chatbot helps them start agritourism businesses

Willie Jones covers transportation for IEEE Spectrum and the history of technology for The Institute.

Alice Dong has created an AI chatbot website that helps Colorado farmers plan and operate agribusinesses that draw visitors to their properties.

Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job.

Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension, CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there.

Xue “Alice” Dong Employer Colorado State University Extension in Logan CountyTitle Extension regional specialistMember grade Senior memberAlma maters Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

Colorado State University Extension in Logan County

Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products.

Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business.

She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside.

“We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in.

Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and theU.N.’s International Telecommunication Union, and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC), and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP).

She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture.

Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors.

As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs.

That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings.

“I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says.

She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career.

She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education.

She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016.

That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020.

After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College, in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator.

She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water.

She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain, helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park.

In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns.

She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds.

Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System, a nationwide network run by land-grant universities, schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states.

The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture, managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties.

The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program, which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship.

Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person.

She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says.

“We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says.

Dong also focuses not on only on whether people use AI, but also on how they use it. In 2026, she and Paul Hill from Utah State University Extension published “From Access to Governance: Generative AI Literacy for Extension Professionals and Small Businesses, and a Governance-Aware Design Framework” in the journal AI. The paper offers a framework for helping Extension professionals and small businesses adopt generative AI responsibly.

In 2025, Dong earned a third master’s degree, in artificial intelligence and machine learning, from CSU Global.

She immediately put those skills to work on agritourism, she says. She built the chatbot in Python, a popular programming language. It answers typed questions, and its user interface looks much like ChatGPT’s, but it works differently. Under the hood, it uses retrieval-augmented generation, a technique that has the AI look up information in a set of trusted documents before it answers. Dong curated that collection from Extension publications, so the chatbot’s answers rest on authoritative sources and are less likely to be made up. She presented the project at NeurIPS 2025 (Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems). The code is openly available on GitHub, so other Extension offices can adapt it.

The bot runs in a web browser rather than as a phone app. Many farmers she works with don’t own a smartphone, Dong says, but nearly all have a computer, tablet, or other gadget that can connect to a website. The bot works on any of them, with no app to download.

Extension specialists “act as a bridge. We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Farmers often ask the bot how to attract visitors and how to write a business plan. A farmer thinking about opening a corn maze, for example, can ask how to price admission, what kind of insurance to carry, and which permits to get. The bot also gives advice on managing risk.

One of her test sites was Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch, in eastern Colorado. Dong documented how the ranch put AI to work in a peer-reviewed case study, “Revolutionizing Agritourism with AI and Machine Learning: A Case Study of Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch in Colorado,” published in 2025 in CABI Tourism Cases.

Surveys and interviews she conducted with other users showed that people find it’s easy to use the bot, learn from it, and act on its advice, she says. She is preparing the full results for publication.

Her work extends beyond agritourism. In 2026, she contributed an AI assistant to Project Pythia, an open-science program funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and led by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR). The AI assistant turns raw airport weather report data into plain-language guidance for farmers and other non-technical users, and it tells users when data is missing rather than guessing.

She also teaches workshops on AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. She has taught her workshop 20 times to more than 200 entrepreneurs and business owners, who came from 32 Colorado counties. In follow-up surveys, 90 percent of participants reported trying at least one new AI task in their business. Some of the workshops take place at a community center run by the Logan County Economic Development Corp., in Sterling. She has also co-hosted the workshops with the Rural Community Assistance Corp., Colorado Startup Week, and Boulder Startup Week. And she occasionally presents them as webinars, so people don’t have to travel.

Her outreach has taught her that many farmers are eager to try new tools, she says. She shows them how simple her chatbot is to use.

She also offers advice to high school students drawn to the field. Extension specialists each have a specialty, such as livestock, natural resources, food systems, or 4-H. Students should pick one based on their passion, she says.

Land-grant universities offer related programs at the bachelor’s and master’s levels. For graduate students, she adds, Extension offers a third career path beyond academia and industry: “You apply advanced skills directly to the communities that need them.”

Dong joined IEEE in 2025 and soon was elevated to senior member. Her professional home is the IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology. She also serves as vice treasurer of the IEEE Denver Section’s Young Professionals group.

IEEE supports all three parts of her job, she says. For research, she presented “Entrepreneur AI Agent: Empowering Small Businesses and Bridging the Digital Divide through Context-Aware Generative AI” at the 2026 IEEE Global Humanitarian Technology Conference (GHTC). For teaching, she has offered to bring her AI workshop to Denver Section members and local entrepreneurs. For service, she reviews papers for IEEE conferences.

IEEE conferences matter most to her, she says: “Through them, I can present my research and network with other researchers in the field.”

She attended the IEEE World Forum on Public Safety Technology in Boulder, Colo., in September 2026. The event, she says, opened her eyes to many new projects underway across IEEE.

Still, she says, her work always points back to the farms and ranches of eastern Colorado. Its people are curious, she says, but they can’t make the leap to new technology alone.

“They really need this kind of a bridge,” she says.

Willie Jones is an associate editor at IEEE Spectrum. In addition to editing and planning daily coverage, he manages several of Spectrum's newsletters and contributes regularly to the monthly Big Picture section that appears in the print edition.

#3257. Microsoft is retiring To Do, and personal users get no replacement

Microsoft To Do’s work users move to Planner, but their tasks won’t follow. Wunderlist’s founder, whose app Microsoft bought and closed, says he would love to buy To Do back.

Microsoft’s support page covers To Do on the web, Windows, Mac, iOS and Android. Its advice to personal users is blunt.

“Choose another task-management application that meets your needs,” Microsoft’s guidance says.

The company announced the change at the end of a long Planner blog post on Wednesday, during its Ignite conference. Windows Latest spotted it the same day.

Existing To Do tasks and lists will not move to Planner. Work users can still see them in Planner until the June deadline, and then lose access. Shared lists, their members and their permissions will not transfer either.

Microsoft has promised a tool to export To Do data before the apps close. It has not published instructions yet. It also warns that exported data may not import into Planner or any other app. Retiring the apps does not by itself schedule the data for deletion, the company says.

Planner also lacks several To Do features. Microsoft does not plan native Planner apps for Windows or Mac. Its web and Teams versions do not offer the same offline access. Private tasks cannot take file attachments for now. List groups have no equivalent, and Microsoft has no plans for printing or emailing a list. The old Tasks feature in classic Outlook, meanwhile, will keep working.

The To Do service and its links to other apps will retire later. Microsoft says it will announce those dates separately.

Microsoft is merging To Do and Planner’s plan types into one system it calls unified plans. One system lets it offer the same features everywhere, the Planner team wrote. It also lets users connect their tasks to Copilot and other agents. At Ignite, Microsoft also put Office inside Copilot, pitched Copilot as cheaper than Claude and launched MAI Code 2.

A Microsoft spokesperson acknowledged the gap for home users in a statement to Windows Central.

“We recognize this change will affect customers differently, particularly those using personal Microsoft accounts, and we’re committed to helping them prepare,” said Howard Crow, Microsoft’s director of product for agents and AI.

For many users this is the second move. Microsoft bought 6Wunderkinder, the Berlin startup behind Wunderlist, in 2015 for a reported $100m to $200m. Its team built To Do, and Microsoft shut Wunderlist down in May 2020.

Wunderlist’s founder, Christian Reber, now runs Superlist, which started in 2020. It called itself “the natural successor” and already offers a To Do importer, GeekWire’s Todd Bishop reported. Reber also replied to the news on X.

“I’d love to buy it back anytime!” Reber wrote.

Rivals moved fast. TickTick posted a migration guide, and Todoist’s chief executive, Amir Salihefendic, called the shutdown “pretty unexpected” on LinkedIn, GeekWire reported. Brad Silverberg, who led Windows 95 development, said he had used To Do daily. He is now looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Microsoft says it will add export instructions, the supported data and any limits to its support page once they are final.

#3256. Report: Apple job listings detail plans for autonomous AI agents

Bloomberg reports that Apple is hiring engineers to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of browsing the web, writing code, and controlling apps on behalf of users. Here are the details.

In a report published today, Bloomberg notes that new job listings on Apple’s website indicate the company’s efforts to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of performing complex tasks on the user’s behalf.

Since the breakout success of OpenClaw, autonomous AI agents have become increasingly popular, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and SpaceXSI among those offering their own solutions.

The increasing popularity of these agents has put Apple under pressure to catch up, while the company has also introduced new restrictions on how third-party AI agents can access and control Macs.

Over at the App Store, Meta’s Muse has become one of the fastest-growing apps in US history, surpassing 10 million downloads in just 40 days, according to Sensor Tower, and spending weeks at the top of the charts. As of today, it sits at No. 2 among free apps, behind TikTok.

And while there are differences in how phone-based and computer-based agents operate, these systems can usually work together, coordinating tasks across devices and apps to accomplish increasingly complex goals.

Back to Bloomberg’s report, it notes Apple recently posted new job listings that offer a closer look at its plans to develop autonomous AI agents:

In one, Apple said it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”

The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

Today’s report on the new job listings comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Apple wants to make Siri more like an autonomous AI agent, with the ability to proactively carry out tasks without requiring users to initiate every step. According to Mark Gurman, the company could introduce these capabilities as soon as next year.

With the new job listings, Apple has offered a more detailed look at its plans for autonomous AI agents, although the language suggests that development is still in its early stages.

Of course, given how quickly the technology is evolving, the landscape could look very different by the time Apple is ready to introduce its own solution next year, much like how the industry had already moved toward autonomous agents by the time Apple finally launched its long-awaited Siri AI overhaul.

You know the cheap, good, quick scale? If you want cheap and quick, it's not gonna be good, etc etc. The Soundcore P31i are all three. They're super cheap, they're super good, and they can be delivered by Amazon Prime quickly. Take that, engineers. Or thought-experimenters.

Lamborghini-orange earbuds without the eye-watering Italian price tag; and they're more reliable. They won't leave you on the side of the road with a busted transmission — but the CMF Buds Pro 2 will try to feed you ChatGPT. Somehow, the transmission issues feel less bad. Thanks, Nothing.

Simple, uncompromising earbuds is probably how some would describe the Liberty 5 earbuds. But I'm not 'some' — the Liberty 5 are good, but boring. And they thrust AI down your throat. Stahp. Can't deny the value for under $100, though. This is a great deal.

The Nothing Ear (3) are the business. They look wicked, I love their sound and... oh, what's this? Oh God, ChatGPT integration. At least the cool case that doubles as a higher-quality call mic is cool. And $50 off? I reckon I can forgive the chatbot thing.

The Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro have a Guinness World Record, I'm told, for sound quality. Take that for what it's worth (not much) — instead, take our word for it. These are great buds with excellent sound quality and... oh, come on now. AI integration. $40 off takes the sting out.

Now we're talking. There's no AI chatbot assistant or anything artificial here — just a great pair of buds. Previous gen they might be, but they've still got it where it counts. Namely, sick sound quality and good battery life. Oh, and Sony's app is really good.

Samsung's at it again, stealing Apple's naming convention. They've stolen the shape too — and then tossed in AI integration (I am, as we speak, mid-AI earbuds breakdown). At least the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro sound excellent and pair very well with Samsung Galaxy devices. And $70 off? Black Friday, you spoil us.

You a fitness freak? Gotta get your sweat on? Then the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are the Black Friday earbuds for you. Their hooks make them stay super solidly in your ears, and they sound great. And they're orange. For $70 off? Please, and thank you.

Do you know how I like to block out the sound of crying children on the bus? If I forget to charge these, then I stick my fingers in my ears and glare angrily at the poor parents — but mostly I use the epic noise-canceling Bose has built into the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2. You can too now, with $70 off this Black Friday.

I haven't talked about AI for at least three entries on the list now — and we're going to continue this winning streak with Sony's flagship buds. The WF-1000XM6 are a great pair of earbuds with excellent noise canceling and amazing sound quality. And they don't thrust some form of chatbot down your throat. Bliss.

#3254. I Don’t Trust Visual Recordings Anymore. But One Day I Will Again

We will have to label our content to prove its authenticity

Hany Farid is a computer science professor at Dartmouth College, in Hanover, N.H.

In March of this year, a flurry of emails and text messages from a half dozen reporters around the world disrupted my quiet Saturday morning. An Iranian news agency had aired a week-old video of what appeared to be a U.S.-made Tomahawk missile hitting a school. News reports claimed that the strike killed more than 175 people, most of them children. The U.S. president and military denied responsibility. In the age of generative AI and all things deepfake, everyone—including me—was skeptical of the video’s authenticity.

I get this type of request a lot. For the past three decades, I’ve been developing mathematical and computational techniques to analyze and detect manipulation in digital media. Over this time, I think it’s fair to say that I, like most people, have approached visual recordings with a “presumption of authenticity”: If a skeptic claims that a recording is fake, the burden of proof is on them.

In today’s world of generative AI, however, I think we need to shift this stance to a “presumption of fake.” That is, the burden is now on the creator to prove that their content is real. While this new stance may seem unfair to legitimate creators, I think it both reflects reality and points to a future where we will once again be able to trust that most online media is what it appears to be.

Even last March, I was already tilting toward a presumption of fake. My initial response to the reporters was something along the lines of, “I am suspicious of the video because the quality is low, it emerged weeks after the bombing, and it is only being distributed by an Iranian news agency with a less-than-stellar record of accurate reporting.”

Given the potential implications—if the video was indeed real, however, I resigned myself to spending my Saturday morning analyzing it.

I first reasoned that if the Tomahawk missile was digitally added to each frame of the video without taking into consideration the camera motion, we might see a physically implausible missile path. So I aligned the video frames using a stationary background landmark as a reference. In the updated video, the missile did, in fact, move in a nearly linear trajectory. (See the yellow dots in the composite shown below.)

I next asked if the size (in pixels) of the missile in the video was plausible. Under some reasonable assumptions, I estimated that the missile in the video corresponded to a 6-meter Tomahawk at a distance of approximately 100 meters. The distance seemed plausible from the scene and was also consistent with the delay of 0.3 seconds from visible impact to the sound of impact, given that sound travels at 343 meters per second.

A composite photo composed of frames from a video of the Tomahawk strike reveals the missile’s trajectory.Hany Farid; Source: Mehr News

Despite the mounting evidence, though, I struggled to refine my answer for the reporters.

My skepticism was fueled by a recent study I worked on with colleagues at the University of California, Berkeley, that showed how hard it is to distinguish real from fake videos. Observers are now so suspicious of videos in general that they have trouble convincing themselves that a video is real.

But after a few more hours and a few more analyses with the missile video, I finally decided that it was authentic, and I gave the reporters my updated view.

This analysis marked a turning point for me. I realized I was just like the participants in our study: The lack of artifacts was not enough to readily convince me a video is real. I had flipped from a presumption of real to a presumption of fake.

When the visual record is no longer reliable, what can we do?

The types of forensic analyses that I routinely perform do not currently operate at internet scale and speed. But provenance signals can. These signals include content credentials and watermarks that are inserted or embedded at the time of creation or recording.

Credentials that follow the C2PA standard, for example, attach a cryptographically signed manifest to a photo or video at the moment of capture; this metadata records the device, the time and location of the recording, and any subsequent edits. Because the manifest is signed, any tampering with either the content or its history can be detected later by machine. Watermarks, like Google’s SynthID, embed an imperceptible signal directly into the pixels or audio samples that identifies the content’s origin.

Apple recently took these ideas a step further. On some of its newest iPhones, the camera sensor can cryptographically sign the raw pixel data as it’s captured. That signed data is then developed into a reference image saved alongside the normal, editable photo. Anyone can then compare the two and see exactly what, if anything, was changed.

These provenance signals are often criticized as being only a partial solution or vulnerable to attack. This is true if we think of them as mechanisms for catching bad actors. But that’s not what they’re supposed to do. Their purpose is to let good actors prove that their audiovisual recording is what it claims to be.

Provenance signals thus need not be adversary-proof. Instead, these signals are part of a new reality in which consumers, journalists, and the courts must adapt to a presumption of fakeness. If enough good actors adopt these mechanisms, they can begin to drown out bad actors. In other words, we have to switch from a model of “catch the bad actors” to “empower the good actors.”

This switch from trust to distrust of digital media has expanded to include routine video calls.

In September 2024, for example, Senator Ben Cardin (D-Md.), then chair of the Foreign Relations Committee, received a video meeting request from Dmytro Kuleba, who until a few weeks earlier had been Ukraine’s foreign minister. During the call, Cardin became suspicious when, out of character, Kuleba pressed him on whether the U.S. should allow Ukraine to fire long-range missiles into Russia. Cardin ended the call. Later, the State Department confirmed that Kuleba had never requested the meeting, and the Senate security office warned staff that foreign adversaries, possibly Russian, would likely try similar faked meetings again.

All it takes to conduct this type of impersonation is a face swap or avatar deepfake, along with voice conversion, both of which substitute the speaker’s face and voice for deepfaked versions in real time. These technologies are readily available in commercial products and open-source libraries and run on nothing more powerful than a modern laptop.

This video illustrates the current state of face-swap deepfakes.

Farid’s Company GetReal Shows How Real Deepfake Videos Look Today Your browser does not support the video tag. Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetReal

Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetReal

Unlike the Tomahawk video, which I could sit with for a morning analyzing frame by frame, a live video call offers no time for human analysis. On the other hand, real-time deepfakes pose new challenges for their creators: A fake video call has to be generated at around 24 frames per second to fool the eye into perceiving realistic motion. As a result, the deepfake-video-call software has to take shortcuts, such as simplifying faces and how they interact with their surroundings, and allowing some drift between audio and video or between video frames. The human eye doesn’t notice the shortcuts, but we can forensically expose them.

Provenance signals should eventually play a role here. Video-calling software could apply the same cryptographic signing to each frame of a live video stream that Apple now applies to still photographs. A face swap necessarily occurs between a speaker’s camera and the videoconferencing software, and so the software could verify in real time whether the frames it’s receiving were signed by a physical camera sensor or whether they were altered in transit. As before, the burden shifts from catching the impersonator to allowing real participants to prove they are who they claim to be.

For the first two decades of the digital revolution, forensic analysis—finding the telltale traces of manipulation—was enough to adjudicate most questions of authenticity. The AI revolution, however, has changed the scale and speed of manipulation beyond what forensics alone can handle. To believe a recording is real now, it must also carry a provenance signal from the point of recording. The two approaches work together, with provenance allowing good actors to be trusted, while forensic analyses root out the bad actors.

Hany Farid is a computer science professor at Dartmouth College, in Hanover, N.H. About 10 years ago, he randomly picked up a book in the library on the federal rules of evidence and was astonished to learn that courts made no distinction between photos from negatives and digital photos, even though the latter can be easily altered. “Digital photography was just getting started,” Farid says. “I realized this was really going to be a huge problem.” Since then digital photo forensics has become the focus of his research. He now frequently testifies in U.S. courts and advises law enforcement agencies. “All that from picking up a book,” he says.

The emerging authentication and provenance systems make a lot of sense for mainstream uses. I get the impression we'll still need forensic analysis for plenty of edge cases, though. People using older hardware or anyone trying to capture evidence in situations where it isn't safe to share clues about the media's origin come to mind.

#3252. Cognition in talks to raise at a $75bn valuation, Bloomberg reports

Existing backers lead interest in the new Cognition funding, Bloomberg reports. It would be the Devin maker’s third round of 2026, after more than $3bn raised so far.

Scott Wu, co-founder and chief executive of Cognition

Cognition, the startup behind the AI coding agent Devin, is in talks to raise money at a $75bn valuation, two months after its last round. Bloomberg’s Rebecca Torrence reported the talks on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.

The company is weighing a raise of $2bn or more, according to Bloomberg. The talks are ongoing and the details could change. TNW has not independently verified the report.

Most of the interest has come from current backers, Bloomberg reported. Avenir, Accel, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Lux Capital and Bessemer Venture Partners are in talks to take part, some of the people said.

Avenir, Accel and Lux declined to comment to Bloomberg. Bessemer, Lightspeed and Cognition did not respond to its requests.

A completed deal would be Cognition’s third round this year. It has already raised more than $3bn in 2026, including over $2bn at a $48bn valuation in September. That round nearly doubled its value in 15 weeks, after a $26bn round in May.

The figure sits inside the range reported last month. In October, Business Insider’s Katie Roof reported investor offers valuing Cognition at $70bn to $80bn.

Investors have poured money into startups building AI agents for software work. Devin competes with Cursor, which SpaceX bought for $60bn. Days after that deal closed, SpaceX reportedly approached Cognition about a takeover too.

Cognition sells to companies including Citigroup and Nvidia. In September it said it was on track for $1bn in annualised revenue, roughly double its run rate four months earlier. This month it signed an alliance with McKinsey to sell Devin to large firms.

The size of the raises has drawn criticism. Ed Zitron, a critic of the AI industry’s spending, questioned the round on X.

“Why does this company need $5bn in the space of a year,” Zitron wrote.

#3251. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 stocks for their solid growth potential

Investors are closely monitoring earnings releases of artificial intelligence companies amid concerns about the durability of high spending and demand. While quarterly results provide key insights into a company's performance and execution, it is prudent to focus on long-term prospects and look beyond short-term fluctuations.

Top Wall Street analysts can help investors pick stocks with attractive long-term prospects as their assessments are backed by in-depth research of a company's fundamentals and growth opportunities.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

AI-powered data analytics provider Palantir Technologies is this week's first pick. The company reported market-beating second-quarter results. Moreover, Palantir raised its full-year guidance and now expects U.S. commercial business revenue to grow by at least 134%.

Following the Q2 print, Bank of America analyst Mariana Perez Mora reiterated a buy rating on PLTR stock with a price target of $255. Mora said that Palantir's performance reflects the success of its AI strategy, which focuses on delivering the right infrastructure to customers and ensuring better outcomes.

"The main driver continues to be the U.S. commercial business, which now represents almost 40% of total (vs. 30% a year ago and just 20% a couple of years back)," noted Mora.

The five-star analyst highlighted the 149% growth in Palantir's U.S. commercial business in Q2 2026 and the expansion in its customer base and engagement levels, with clients pursuing more integrated relationships. Mora noted that the U.S. commercial customer count increased 35% year-over-year to 653, with trailing twelve months revenue per customer surging 76% to $3.5 million in the second quarter.

Citing strength across Palantir's commercial and government segments, Mora increased her sales and earnings per share estimates for 2026-2028. The analyst attributed the increase in her estimates to the growth in the commercial business, backed by stronger total contract value in the second quarter.

Mora ranks No. 444 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 32.6%. See Palantir Insider Trading Activity on TipRanks.

E-commerce and cloud computing giant Amazon impressed investors with its strong second-quarter results. Revenue from the company's Amazon Web Services (AWS) cloud business surged 37%, marking the unit's fastest growth since 2021.

In reaction to the Q2 2026 performance, JPMorgan analyst Doug Anmuth reiterated a buy rating on Amazon stock and raised his price target to $365 from $330, saying that it remains the firm's Best Idea. Anmuth highlighted that the company's forex-neutral top-line growth accelerated to 20% in Q2 2026, the fastest in 20 quarters. He added that the top line gained from acceleration across both AWS and stores.

The five-star analyst noted that AWS growth of 37% was the fastest in 18 quarters, with backlog jumping nearly 2.5x year-over-year and 36% sequentially to $496 billion. Amazon's backlog gained from robust demand across both core workloads and AI adoption. Anmuth also observed the strength in AWS' AI and chips businesses, Graviton revenue commitments, and AWS' core business.

Notably, Anmuth believes that the core AWS business is highly correlated to AI revenue, and he expects further strengthening of this relationship as more AI workloads move into full-scale production and fuel higher demand. Overall, the analyst is more optimistic on Amazon following Q2 results and raised his 2026 and 2027 sales estimates by about 1% to 2% and operating income by about 5% to 7%.

"Importantly, management emphasized that the [return on invested capital] on its AI investments is compelling and it has a clear line-of-sight to strong financial returns," said Anmuth.

Anmuth ranks No. 717 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 10.5%. See Amazon Statistics on TipRanks.

Moving on to Lam Research, a supplier of semiconductor manufacturing equipment and services. Thanks to AI-driven demand, the company delivered better-than-anticipated fiscal fourth quarter results.

In reaction to the solid results, Oppenheimer analyst Edward Yang reaffirmed a buy rating on LRCX stock with a price target of $400. Yang stated that Lam Research exceeded June-quarter expectations despite the high bar, driven by strong performance of the Customer Support Business Group and doubling of NAND revenue from the prior quarter. He also cited the improvement in Q4 FY26 gross margin.

The five-star analyst highlighted that Lam Research's September-quarter revenue and EPS outlook exceeded the Street's expectations by mid-teens percentages. Yang added that the company increased its wafer fabrication equipment spending outlook to the low-$150 billion range, up from its prior $140 billion estimate.

Importantly, Yang noted that Lam Research called calendar year 2027 "extraordinary," citing persistent supply shortages and the addition of 8 to 10 new fabrication plants. The analyst raised his 2027 revenue and EPS estimates by 7% and 9% to $33 billion and $8.88, respectively. Yang also increased his 2028 revenue and EPS estimates by 7% and 8% to $36.6 billion and $9.89, respectively.

"It's the cleanest way to play AI-driven 3D scaling across memory, foundry/logic, and packaging," said Yang about LRCX.

Yang ranks No. 256 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 56.4%. See Lam Research Technical Analysis on TipRanks.

#3250. macOS 27.3 public beta 2 now available, here’s everything new

After releasing developer beta 2 of macOS 27.3 earlier this week, the company is now rolling out the public beta for users looking to try the new features ahead of next month’s official release. Here’s what’s coming.

Those came alongside several new features and tools on macOS 27.3 beta 1, including vertical tabs and adaptive dark mode in Safari, native Live Activities support, Markdown rendering in Quick Look, additional checks for potentially harmful content shared through iCloud links, and Siri AI support for Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

And speaking of Siri AI, macOS 27.3 also expands the assistant’s capabilities across Apple’s own apps, allowing users to perform more complex actions in Messages, Music, Calendar, Photos, and Reminders, as well as manage files and folders. Apple is also introducing new tools for third-party developers to build more advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions.

While macOS 27.2 was a rather uneventful update, macOS 27.3 is shaping up to be the biggest update since the release of macOS 27, and users on the public beta can now try out these new features ahead of their official release.

The release build for macOS 27.3 public beta 2 is 26C5047e, which matches the developer build.

If you’d like to join Apple’s free public beta program, visit beta.apple.com.

Did you spot anything new in today’s beta? Let us know in the comments.

#3248. Databricks in early talks to raise at a $225bn valuation, WSJ reports

Chief executive Ali Ghodsi says Databricks will go public, but not during AI’s ups and downs. The Databricks valuation would be nearly 20% above August’s $190bn.

Ali Ghodsi, co-founder and chief executive of Databricks

Databricks is in early talks to raise several billion dollars at a valuation of about $225bn, The Wall Street Journal’s Meghan Bobrowsky and Kate Clark reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. That would be nearly 20% above the $190bn valuation the data company reached in August.

The talks are ongoing and the terms could still change, according to the Journal. TNW has not independently verified the report.

The new money would come while Databricks stays private. Its chief executive, Ali Ghodsi, explained why in a recent interview on the All-In podcast.

“We will go public. We are going to be public, but right now I think during this transition period of AI there’s just too much up and down, and I think it’s distracting to companies,” Ghodsi told All-In.

Databricks closed a $5bn round at $190bn in August. It said then that it had passed a $7bn revenue run rate, the Journal reported.

Ghodsi told All-In the business is growing 70% to 80% a year, and that he wants more. He would like growth of 100%, “way over 100”, he said.

The company has added AI products this year. They include an agent called Genie One, which answers questions from a company’s business data, and Unity Gateway, which gives customers access to models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Genie also reached Slack this month, in a version that answers data questions inside the chat app.

Its investors include Coatue Management, Andreessen Horowitz, NEA, Insight Partners, Fidelity and J.P. Morgan Asset Management, according to the Journal.

The Journal calls Databricks a candidate for a near-term listing. Investors say a strong showing by Anthropic, whose stock ended its first week worth $1.6tn, could unleash a wave of AI listings, the paper reported.

Ghodsi weighed both sides on All-In. A listing brings access to capital and a quarterly marketing moment, he said. Staying private means Databricks must arrange its own tender offers for staff every year. He said employees have never used up all the money set aside for them.

His worry is volatility. When a stock falls, he said, staff effectively take a pay cut, and some leave before the price recovers.

Ghodsi also said he believes AI has already reached artificial general intelligence, by the definition his Berkeley lab used around 2010. He put the risk of AI wiping out humanity close to zero, and named cyberattacks as the real danger.

“I think the cyber risk is real and really bad things can happen with that,” he said.

#3246. LiberNovo’s Black Friday sale takes up to 42% off ergonomic chairs

You can spend plenty of time getting your Mac, display, and desk just right. But what about the chair you use every day? Between typing, taking video calls, and leaning back to watch something, your position changes throughout the day. Your chair should be able to keep up.

That’s the idea behind LiberNovo’s ergonomic chairs, which combine support that moves with you and a choice of sizes, including the Maxis range for bigger and taller users. For Black Friday, LiberNovo is taking up to 42% off in the U.S., with chairs starting at $609 and offers running November 19–30.

Adjusting a chair for your desk is one thing. Keeping that support as you change position is another. LiberNovo’s Dynamic Support System links the neck support, backrest, armrests, and seat so they move together as you recline.

The Bionic FlexFit Backrest adds eight flexible panels that contour independently. Rather than relying on a single rigid backrest, the design lets different sections follow your back as you shift or turn. Once you’ve adjusted the chair to fit, the system is designed to maintain contact through those movements with fewer manual readjustments.

Both the Omni and Maxis families offer five recline positions: 105, 115, 125, 135, and 160 degrees. That gives you options for desk work, a more relaxed position for watching a video, and a deeper recline for a break.

A higher weight limit is only part of finding a chair that fits. Taller users also need enough seat depth, a headrest that reaches the right spot, and armrests with room to adjust.

The LiberNovo Maxis range addresses those details with a 52 cm seat depth, a wider backrest with a flared base, and an extended-travel headrest with 140 mm of vertical adjustment and 120 mm of front-to-back adjustment. Its armrests sit lower and offer a wider, longer adjustment range to accommodate larger builds.

LiberNovo recommends Maxis for users approximately 5 feet 10 inches to 6 feet 7 inches tall, with a maximum supported weight of 399 pounds. Maxis is certified to BIFMA X5.11. The seat cushion uses firmer support at the rear and a softer front edge, while a six-spring Controlled Recline System is designed to build resistance progressively as you lean back.

For a shallower seat, the Omni family offers 45 cm and 48 cm configurations. Choosing between the two families starts with fit, then comes down to which features you want.

There are three feature tiers in each family. Omni SE and Maxis Manual offer manually adjusted lumbar support, without a motor or battery. Both retain the flexible backrest, dynamic support, and five recline positions.

The Maxis Electric includes motorized lumbar adjustment and OmniStretch, a five-minute powered stretch sequence used in deep recline.

Omni Pro and Maxis Airflow add Active AirFlow seat ventilation. A fan draws air through the cushion to carry heat away, and an occupancy sensor pauses the fan when you stand up. These models also include a larger 3,000 mAh rechargeable battery.

LiberNovo’s warranty covers the frame and structural components for six years, and electronic components for two years.

#3245. Samsung names new chip and phone bosses amid a reported China shipment halt

TM Roh hands the Galaxy business to Won-Joon Choi in a Samsung leadership change. Samsung and TSMC have paused some China orders for US licences, the FT reports.

Samsung Electronics’ Digital City campus in Suwon, South Korea

Samsung Electronics has named new heads for its memory chip and smartphone businesses. The changes came in a week when it reportedly paused some chip shipments to China under new US export rules. The company announced the changes on Friday in Korea.

Sang Joon Hwang will run the memory business, and Won-Joon Choi takes over Mobile eXperience, the unit behind Galaxy phones, Samsung said in a newsroom statement. Co-chief executives Young Hyun Jun and TM Roh keep their roles.

Samsung promoted Hwang to president. He previously led memory development, including DRAM and the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used in AI chips. Samsung said it expects him to strengthen its memory products for the AI era. It reportedly plans to make HBM parts for AMD and Nvidia at a second Texas fab.

Sangyeun Cho, who ran Samsung’s chip business in the Americas, becomes president of System LSI, its chip design unit. Jong Myeong Lee, the former head of process development, becomes chief technology officer of the Device Solutions division, which makes Samsung’s chips.

Choi has been chief operating officer of the mobile unit since March 2025 and led the launches of the Galaxy S26 and Galaxy Z Fold8. Roh had run the mobile business for most of the last seven years, 9to5Google noted. He stays in charge of the Device eXperience division, which includes phones and TVs.

Earlier this week, the Financial Times reported that Samsung and TSMC had suspended some shipments to Chinese customers. Both are applying for licences from the US Commerce Department under new rules, the FT reported.

The rules close a route that let Chinese designers order advanced chips through third-party packaging and testing firms. They also remove an exemption for chips not meant for AI, according to the FT. They arrived in the same week as US limits on Chinese remote access to AI chips in overseas data centres.

Samsung’s Chinese customers include ByteDance and Baidu’s chip unit Kunlun, while TSMC makes phone chips for Xiaomi, the FT reported. It is unclear which customers have been told to wait. An industry insider told the FT that Washington will likely approve licences for consumer smartphone chips. The process could still cause delays. TNW has not independently verified the report.

Chinese firms have already warned about the curbs. Tencent and Alibaba said this week the rules will slow growth in AI.

Some data centre operators that serve China have also been hit. Shares in Japan’s Datasection have fallen 47% since Monday, and it warned annual revenue could be up to 89% below its forecast, The Telegraph reported.

Samsung did not link its leadership changes to the export rules. Its statement says it wants the new team to strengthen its future competitiveness in semiconductors.

#3243. WhatsApp is raising group chat limit to 1,500 participants

WhatsApp is gradually rolling out an increase to its group chat limit, allowing up to 1,500 participants to join in, instead of the previous 1,024 cap. Here are the details.

While there are exceptions, there are generally two kinds of WhatsApp users: those who hate group chats, and those who can’t seem to be in enough of them.

If you’re in the second category, you’re likely aware that WhatsApp has steadily increased the number of participants allowed in group chats over the years, jumping from 100 to 256 in 2016, then to 512 and, soon after, to 1,024 in 2022.

Now, as spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is once again expanding that limit, raising the maximum number of participants in a group chat to 1,500.

According to the website, the new limit is rolling out to users on iOS and Android, though the rollout is gradual, meaning “not every account will see the higher limit immediately.”

WhatsApp is automatically updating existing groups to support the new limit. This means that admins do not need to take any action to unlock the higher capacity. As soon as the update becomes available to their accounts, their groups will support up to 1500 members. As a result, the update lets admins add up to 476 new members to their existing groups.

This rollout comes as WhatsApp has been working to make group chats easier to manage. Just last month, the company announced four new features, including the ability to pin messages indefinitely, share status updates within groups, filter conversations by mentions and replies, and share recent message history with new members after they join.

#3242. Etsy will revise its AI training terms after sellers close their shops

The Etsy AI terms let it and its partners train models on sellers’ work from 16 December. Sellers who ran shops for up to 13 years have walked out.

Etsy says it will revise its new terms of use. Longtime sellers had begun closing their shops over a clause that lets it use their work to train AI. The New York Times’ Reggie Ugwu reported the walkouts and the company’s retreat on Friday.

The new terms take effect on 16 December. They let Etsy and its partners use sellers’ content to build and train AI. The previous version had no clause about AI, the Times reported. The key line reads:

Etsy and its “third party partners and vendors” may use sellers’ content to “develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies.”

Several sellers who had run shops for years said they were leaving. Illustrator Aaron Millard said on Instagram he was deleting the shop he had run for nearly a decade. He wrote that sellers had no way to opt out.

Kristen and Geoff Zephyrus deleted their shop too. They have sold home goods and stationery on Etsy for 13 years as Cognitive Surplus.

“For Etsy to be helping to train algorithms with our human content is just unimaginably awful,” Kristen Zephyrus told the Times.

James Ossman, Etsy’s vice president for customer operations, answered sellers in a post on Etsy’s website this week.

Etsy will not “use your content to train A.I. models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity,” Ossman wrote.

He said third parties get access to sellers’ content for uses such as fraud detection and advertising. In a statement to the Times, he said Etsy would send sellers the revised terms soon. Sellers’ creative work belongs to them, he added.

Some critics doubt the reassurance. Tyler Wilde, PC Gamer’s US editor-in-chief, wrote an opinion piece on the clause. To him, it reads like blanket permission to train AI on user content for any purpose. He argued that Etsy should leave every seller out of AI training by default.

Etsy has faced seller protests before. In 2022, more than 20,000 sellers went on strike over a fee rise. Etsy had raised its basic sales fee from 5% to 6.5%. In October, it tightened its rules on low-quality AI content after users complained, the Times reported.

The company cut 12% of its staff in August. The dispute also lands amid wider pushback against AI. Donald Trump Jr told Axios this week that investors had underestimated the AI backlash. Elton John urged Australia to protect artists from AI at the Aria awards.

#3239. SK Hynix will become Kioxia’s largest shareholder through a bond swap

The SK Hynix Kioxia stake comes from converting bonds bought in 2018, with no new money beyond a small payment to Bain. Both firms say Kioxia stays independent.

SK hynix’s exhibition booth at the Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) conference

SK Hynix will become the largest shareholder in Kioxia, its Japanese rival in flash memory, by converting bonds it has held since 2018 into shares. It will hold an indirect stake of about 14.1%, it said in a filing on Friday.

Bloomberg’s Yoolim Lee first reported the filing. The move puts SK Hynix ahead of Toshiba, Kioxia’s former parent, which held 10.46% in early November, according to Korea JoongAng Daily.

SPC2 is a special-purpose company set up for the 2018 deal. SK Hynix will convert 129bn yen ($810m) of its bonds into 129,000 shares. It will also buy Bain Capital’s remaining 1,001 SPC2 shares for 100m yen. The steps close in December, leaving SK Hynix as SPC2’s sole owner.

Apart from the payment to Bain, the deal adds no new money, MoneyToday reported, citing the company. SK Hynix called it a follow-up step after it sold out of a separate Kioxia fund in June. Gains from that sale funded about 7tn won ($5.2bn) of special dividends in the third quarter.

SK Hynix joined the Bain-led group that bought Kioxia, then Toshiba Memory, in 2018. It put in 395bn yen at the time.

Both companies make NAND, the chips used for storage in phones and AI servers. SK Hynix held 19% of the global NAND market in the second quarter and Kioxia 14%, according to Counterpoint figures cited by Bloomberg. Together that tops market leader Samsung’s 28%.

The 2018 deal caps SK Hynix at 15% of Kioxia’s voting shares until 2028, unless Kioxia agrees otherwise. Kioxia lists the stake as a risk factor in its annual report, citing a possible conflict of interest, Bloomberg reported.

Both sides say nothing changes in how Kioxia is run. A Kioxia spokesperson said its management will stay independent.

“We currently have no plans to further buy or sell shares in Kioxia. We will continue to respect Kioxia’s independent management going forward,” an SK Hynix official said.

Masahiro Wakasugi of Bloomberg Intelligence sees little change in the short run.

The move is “unlikely to materially change near-term NAND competition,” Wakasugi wrote.

The stake still gives SK Hynix some say over big decisions, he added. That includes the power to oppose a possible deal between Kioxia and Sandisk.

Separately, SoftBank’s Masayoshi Son reportedly explored a buyout of SK Hynix itself. The Korean company reported a 632% profit jump in October, even as memory stocks slid.

#3237. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for steady income

The stock market continues to grapple with volatility amid geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom. Given this uncertainty, investors looking for steady income can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios.

Tracking the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help investors pick the right dividend stocks, as these experts assign their ratings after an in-depth analysis of a company's financials and ability to pay dividends consistently.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Downstream energy company Phillips 66 (PSX) is this week's first dividend pick. With a quarterly dividend $1.27 per share (annualized dividend of $5.08), PSX offers a yield of 2.25%. The company recently reported solid Q2 earnings, as the Middle East conflict affected global supplies and drove up refining margins.

Following the Q2 print, TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman reiterated a buy rating on Phillips 66 and raised his price target to $255 from $240, reflecting higher 2026 earnings expectations and lower interest expense next year.

Gabelman highlighted the quarter-over-quarter reduction in Phillips 66's net debt, noting management's optimism at achieving its estimated $15.5 billion net debt target one year ahead of schedule. The 5-star analyst expects the company to end 2026 with a net debt of $14.6 billion.

"The [balance sheet] improvement could re-establish PSX as a go-to defensive refiner," said Gabelman.

Management agreed that PSX's payout ratio lagged year-to-date, but expects buybacks to increase in the second half. Gabelman said Phillps indicated the possibility of a larger dividend hike following an annual increase of 5% over the past two years.

Gabelman ranks No. 554 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 66% of the time, delivering an average return of 14.9%. See Phillips 66 Statistics on TipRanks.

Crescent Energy (CRGY) is an exploration and production company with activities focused in the Eagle Ford, Permian and Uinta Basins. Earlier this month, the company reported better-than-expected Q2 earnings and announced a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share, payable on August 31. At an annualized dividend of $0.48 per share, CRGY boasts a dividend yield of about 4%.

In reaction to Q2 results, Evercore analyst Stephen Richardson reaffirmed a buy rating on Crescent Energy stock with a price target of $18. He noted continued strength in the company's performance, with second-quarter oil production and cash flow surpassing the Street's expectations.

"CRGY's cash flow exceeded expectations by 10%, reinforcing its trajectory of capital efficiency," said Richardson.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that Crescent raised its full-year oil production guidance, citing the effective integration of the Vital Energy acquisition. Specifically, Crescent tripled its synergy target from the Vital Energy deal to as much as $300 million, significantly reducing the effective purchase price. This reflects Crescent's solid execution following the acquisition, Richardson said.

Additionally, the analyst noted that Crescent's capital spending is and heading toward the lower end of management's prior guidance, indicating disciplined financial controls.

Richardson ranks No. 579 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 65% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.5%. See Crescent Energy Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Finally, Viper Energy (VNOM) is effectively controlled by Diamondback Energy. Viper owns and acquires mineral and royalty interests in oil-weighted basins, mainly the Permian in West Texas. Viper recently announced its Q2 2026 results and declared a 32% hike in its base dividend, effective in the third quarter of 2026. The new base dividend indicates a 4.5% annualized yield.

Viper also removed its quarterly commitment to return at least 75% of cash available for distribution. The company believes that this move will ensure increased flexibility to make opportunistic share repurchases and pursue accretive mergers and acquisitions.

Following the Q2 results, TD Cowen analyst Aaron Bilkoski reiterated a buy rating on Viper, slightly raising his price target to $59 from $58. Bilkoski said Viper's solid Q2 performance supports his view that the strength in oil prices and rising operator activity are driving higher production.

"Viper has delivered, and we forecast will continue to deliver, one of the highest production per share growth profiles in our royalty universe" through the end of 2027, said Bilkoski. He believes Viper deserves a premium valuation, given its above-average growth.

The 5-star analyst said that while the biggest surprise in the quarter was Viper's revision to its shareholder return framework, he doesn't believe that the move indicates a significant change to its underlying strategy. Under the new framework, a larger portion of excess free cash flow is expected to be allocated to share repurchases than to variable dividends, Bilkoski said.

Bilkoski ranks No. 719 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 12%. See Viper Energy Financials on TipRanks.

#3236. iPhone Air 2 dummy unit shows off new dual-camera design

Apple is expected to release the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 sometime next spring. Ahead of that launch, new dummy units posted to social media today give us a closer look at the devices, including a big update to the iPhone Air 2.

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

In a post on X, Sonny Dickson shared dummy units of the iPhone Air 2, giving us a glimpse of the new dual-camera system. Meanwhile, the base iPhone 18 looks largely unchanged compared to the iPhone 17.

The first-generation iPhone Air has a single 48MP Main camera. The second-generation model, however, will reportedly add an Ultra Wide camera.

First look at the iPhone 18 Air and iPhone 18 dummy units. The biggest change is the iPhone 18 Air, which now features two rear cameras instead of one, while the standard iPhone 18 retains a design similar to the iPhone 17. pic.twitter.com/MdOVuwPlm3

As expected, the iPhone Air 2 cameras are arranged horizontally across the pill-shaped camera plateau, similar to the iPhone Duo’s arrangement.

In addition to the dual-camera system, the iPhone Air 2 is expected to be powered by the A20 Pro chip. Apple is also reportedly working to improve the battery life. The Information has reported the device will feature a vapor chamber cooling system, which Apple debuted with the iPhone 17 Pro. Another report suggested the device will have a smaller Dynamic Island.

The base model iPhone 18, meanwhile, will reportedly use Apple’s A20 chip. Ming-Chi Kuo has reported it will have 9GB of RAM, up from the iPhone 17’s 8GB. It’s expected to be a modest year-over-year update, with Apple focused on cutting costs.

There’s an awful lot to love about the Nintendo Switch 2. It’s less toy-like than its (excellent) predecessor, has a 1080p screen (up from 720p), and it reaches 4K while docked. The problem? Your existing microSD card will be great for Switch 1 games, but Switch 2 games need faster storage via microSD Express cards.

These carry a premium, but the good news is that they’re seeing significant discounts for Black Friday.

UK gamers can save 15%, netting a 512GB card for £135.99 down from £159.99, while US Switch 2 owners can find an even bigger 24% discount, grabbing a SanDisk option for $98.99.

Switch 2 owners in the United States can save even more, with a 24% discount on this 512GB SanDisk microSD card.

Meanwhile, if you're a British reader, you can pick up this microSD Express card from Lexar, available at a 15% discount.

With so many games now too big for cartridges (leading to the controversial Game Key cards that are basically just a download key), it’s worth reiterating just how hefty some Switch 2 titles can be.

Launch titles like Street Fighter 6 and Cyberpunk 2077: Ultimate Edition came in at 60GB, but things have got progressively more storage-hungry from there.

NBA 2K26 is over 70GB, EA Sports FC 27 is 75GB, and WWE 2K26 is 86GB, while the two Final Fantasy VII Remake titles are around 90GB each. That’s on top of launches this year like The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition, Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, and many more.

Honestly, the Switch 2 has grown to become a haven for great third-party titles, and even if you’ve not invested in fresh storage space, you’ll no doubt find it very welcome as more games arrive, like FromSoftware’s Duskbloods, Maneater 2, and Xenoblade Genesis in 2027.
